text:
🇺🇸 THE AMERICAN CIVIL WAR IN 100 POINTS, FROM START TO FINISH

⛓️ THE ROAD TO WAR
1. 1619: The first enslaved Africans arrive in English Virginia
2. 1787: The Constitution counts an enslaved person as three-fifths of a person
3. 1808: The US bans the import of enslaved people
4. 1820: The Missouri Compromise draws a line on the spread of slavery
5. 1831: Nat Turner leads a slave revolt in Virginia
6. 1850: A new Fugitive Slave Act forces the North to return escaped slaves
7. 1852: Uncle Tom’s Cabin turns millions against slavery
8. 1854: The Kansas-Nebraska Act lets settlers vote on slavery
9. 1856: “Bleeding Kansas” erupts, and a senator is beaten with a cane in the Senate
10. 1857: The Dred Scott ruling says Black Americans cannot be citizens
11. 1859: John Brown raids the arsenal at Harpers Ferry
12. Nov 1860: Abraham Lincoln is elected president

✂️ A NATION SPLITS
13. 20 Dec 1860: South Carolina is the first state to secede
14. Jan–Feb 1861: Six more Deep South states leave the Union
15. Feb 1861: The Confederate States of America is formed
16. Jefferson Davis becomes the Confederate president
17. 4 Mar 1861: Lincoln is sworn in
18. 12 Apr 1861: Confederates fire on Fort Sumter: the war begins
19. Lincoln calls for 75,000 volunteers
20. Four more states join the Confederacy, making 11 in total
21. Richmond, Virginia, becomes the Confederate capital
22. Four slave states stay loyal: Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky and Missouri
23. Lincoln orders a naval blockade of the South
24. The “Anaconda Plan” aims to squeeze the South into surrender

⚔️ 1861–1862
25. 21 Jul 1861: First Battle of Bull Run, a shock Confederate victory
26. Thomas Jackson earns the nickname “Stonewall” at Bull Run
27. Nov 1861: The Trent Affair nearly drags Britain into the war
28. Feb 1862: Grant takes Forts Henry and Donelson, earning the name “Unconditional Surrender” Grant
29. Mar 1862: Monitor vs Virginia, the first battle between ironclad warships
30. Apr 1862: Shiloh leaves about 23,000 casualties in two days
31. Apr 1862: The Confederacy passes the first military draft in American history
32. Apr 1862: The Union captures New Orleans, the South’s biggest city
33. Jun 1862: Robert E. Lee takes command of the Army of Northern Virginia
34. 1862: The Homestead Act and Pacific Railway Act reshape the West
35. Jun–Jul 1862: The Seven Days Battles save Richmond
36. Aug 1862: Second Bull Run, another Confederate win
37. 17 Sep 1862: Antietam, the bloodiest single day in US history, with about 23,000 casualties
38. 22 Sep 1862: Lincoln announces the Emancipation Proclamation
39. Dec 1862: Fredericksburg, a crushing Union defeat

🔥 1863: THE TURNING POINT
40. 1 Jan 1863: The Emancipation Proclamation takes effect
41. Black soldiers begin joining the Union army in large numbers
42. Mar 1863: The Union passes its own draft
43. May 1863: Chancellorsville, Lee’s greatest victory
44. Stonewall Jackson is shot by his own men and dies days later
45. Jun 1863: West Virginia breaks away from Virginia and becomes a state
46. 1–3 Jul 1863: Gettysburg, the largest battle of the war, with about 51,000 casualties
47. 3 Jul 1863: Pickett’s Charge fails at Gettysburg
48. 4 Jul 1863: Vicksburg surrenders and the Union controls the Mississippi
49. Jul 1863: Draft riots rock New York City
50. 18 Jul 1863: The Black 54th Massachusetts storms Fort Wagner
51. Sep 1863: Chickamauga, a Confederate victory in Georgia
52. 19 Nov 1863: The Gettysburg Address, just 272 words long
53. Nov 1863: The Union wins at Chattanooga

🎯 1864: TOTAL WAR
54. Feb 1864: The H.L. Hunley becomes the first submarine to sink a warship
55. Mar 1864: Grant takes command of all Union armies
56. May 1864: The Battle of the Wilderness opens Grant’s Overland Campaign
57. May 1864: Spotsylvania Court House
58. Jun 1864: Cold Harbor, where thousands of Union soldiers fall in one failed assault
59. Jun 1864: The siege of Petersburg begins and lasts over 9 months
60. Jun 1864: Lee’s estate at Arlington becomes a national cemetery
61. Aug 1864: Farragut at Mobile Bay: “Damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead!”
62. 2 Sep 1864: Sherman captures Atlanta
63. Nov 1864: Lincoln is re-elected
64. Nov–Dec 1864: Sherman’s March to the Sea cuts through Georgia
65. Dec 1864: Sherman takes Savannah and offers it to Lincoln as a Christmas gift

🏳️ 1865: THE END
66. 31 Jan 1865: Congress passes the 13th Amendment to end slavery
67. 4 Mar 1865: Lincoln’s second inaugural: “With malice toward none”
68. 2 Apr 1865: Petersburg falls and Richmond is evacuated
69. 3 Apr 1865: Union troops enter Richmond
70. 9 Apr 1865: Lee surrenders to Grant at Appomattox Court House
71. 14 Apr 1865: John Wilkes Booth shoots Lincoln at Ford’s Theatre
72. 15 Apr 1865: Lincoln dies, and Andrew Johnson becomes president
73. 26 Apr 1865: Booth is killed, and General Joseph Johnston surrenders in North Carolina
74. 27 Apr 1865: The steamboat Sultana explodes, killing over 1,000 freed Union prisoners
75. 10 May 1865: Jefferson Davis is captured in Georgia
76. 13 May 1865: Palmito Ranch, Texas, the last battle of the war
77. 19 Jun 1865: Enslaved people in Texas learn they are free: the origin of Juneteenth
78. 23 Jun 1865: Stand Watie, a Cherokee, is the last Confederate general to surrender
79. Nov 1865: The CSS Shenandoah surrenders in Liverpool, the last Confederate unit
80. 6 Dec 1865: The 13th Amendment is ratified, and slavery is abolished

📊 THE WAR IN NUMBERS
81. About 620,000 soldiers died, and new studies say up to 750,000
82. It remains the deadliest war in US history
83. About two-thirds of the dead were killed by disease, not bullets
84. About 2.1 million men fought for the Union
85. An estimated 750,000 to 1 million fought for the Confederacy
86. About 180,000 Black soldiers served in the Union army
87. More than 10,000 battles and skirmishes were fought
88. Surgeons performed an estimated 60,000 amputations
89. Nearly 13,000 Union prisoners died at Andersonville prison in Georgia
90. Hundreds of women disguised themselves as men to fight
91. The Union had about 22 million people; the South about 9 million, including 3.5 million enslaved
92. The North had most of the country’s factories and about 70% of its railways

🏛️ FIRSTS AND LEGACY
93. The first war to be widely photographed, by Mathew Brady and his team
94. Lincoln followed battles by telegraph, a first for a US president
95. Congress created the Medal of Honor, now the highest US military award
96. The US introduced its first federal income tax to pay for the war
97. Clara Barton nursed soldiers and later founded the American Red Cross
98. 1865–1877: Reconstruction tries to rebuild the South
99. The 14th and 15th Amendments grant citizenship and voting rights to Black men
100. Memorial Day began as a day to honour the Civil War dead

text:
Maryland families have been paying for Virginia's data centers on their power bills for over a year now. One Virginia county collected $1.2 billion in taxes off those data centers in a single year.

So when Maryland finally got offered a $5 billion data center of its own, 25,000 people signed a petition to kill it. Once you see the deal, you'd have signed it too.

Maryland and Northern Virginia share the same 13-state power grid, run by an outfit called PJM. Every year PJM holds an auction to lock in enough power for the hottest days, and the price went from $28.92 to $329.17 per megawatt-day in two years. The grid's independent watchdog says data centers caused 63% of the first jump. That's $9.3 billion, and it gets spread across everybody's electric bill, including in states that barely have any data centers. Maryland is one of them. The state's consumer advocate is now fighting another $1.6 billion or so at federal regulators over power lines built to feed Virginia.

Virginia's side of the deal looks a lot better. Loudoun County taxes the actual computers inside its data centers, $4.15 for every $100 of equipment. Those companies swap out servers every few years, so the county keeps taxing fresh hardware over and over. Data centers now cover 39% of Loudoun's budget, and homeowners there pay 80.5 cents per $100 on their houses, down from $1.145 a decade ago.

Maryland wrote the opposite rule. In 2020 the state let counties cut the tax on data center equipment all the way to zero, and Prince George's County passed its own version that November. A few months later the council made data centers by-right, which meant a project could go from application to shovels in the ground in 90 days without the council ever voting on it. One person signed up to testify against that bill. Everybody was stuck at home in the pandemic and barely noticed.

Here's what Landover was actually getting out of it. Back in 2021, the county's own economic development chief pitched a $500 million data center as worth about $66 million in property taxes over 10 years. At that rate a $5 billion campus should bring in something like $66 million a year. The developer's booklet for this one projected $13.7 million.

So picture living a mile from that lot. Your power bill has been climbing to cover data centers in another state. Now an 820-megawatt one is getting approved down the street with no council vote, in a county that already passed a law that could let it off the hook for the biggest tax it would owe, and it's promising about a fifth of what the county's own math said it should pay. I get why people signed.

The sad part is the land is still sitting there. The mall closed in 2002 and came down in 2006. The Commanders' stadium right across the road empties out when the team moves back to D.C. in 2030, and they've agreed to tear it down within 90 days of their first game at the new place. Prince George's is looking at a projected $151 million deficit and could end up with two giant empty lots staring at each other.

Loudoun proved a data center can pay for a big chunk of a county's schools and knock down everyone's property taxes. That only works when the county actually taxes the servers and the power bill doesn't land on the neighbors. Fix those two things and the next lot in Maryland probably gets built.

text:
Your name is Tyler. 38. You live in Bloomington, Minnesota, on a street where the houses don't talk to each other. You live between the two that talk the most. You've been practicing americanmaxxing since you were born. You don't know what it is yet.

On your left, Deb. Blue hair. She/her. Prius. Pride flag, a No Human Is Illegal lawn sign, a Harris sticker nobody peeled off. Deb votes blue, donates monthly, signs everything. Deb practices democratmaxxing. She doesn't know what it's called either.

On your right, Rick. Flagpole. F-350. A Let's Go Brandon sign he repaints every two years, because tradition matters. Rick watches the files nobody releases. Rick practices trumpmaxxing. Same deal. Nobody on this street knows what they practice.

You, you don't practice anything. Politics is two teams fighting over your money, and you noticed it at 22. You never mentioned it again. You do one thing: you move forward.

In 2019 you install cooling systems for server rooms. In 2022 you're the guy they call at 2 a.m. when a data center in Abilene, Texas, overheats. In 2024 you own the company that does it in eleven states. People offer to buy it. You don't sell. A clean conscience is nice. You keep a stronghold instead.

Then the AI boom happens. It happens to you. Every chip someone buys makes your phone ring. Billionaires pour concrete into the Texas heat and you take your cut. Your family doesn't understand your job. You stopped explaining in 2023.

Texas gets hot, Minnesota gets weird. You move to Texas. Deb posts about the climate. Rick posts about the border. You post the invoice.

Texas is good. Texas is a data center with a flag. You work, you lift, you learn Spanish from the crew. Your taxes go down. Your truck goes up. Nobody asks who you voted for. It never comes up. You think that's the whole point of the country.

Then Florida, 2026. A villa with a view of the water. The realtor is Dominican. The street is Venezuelans, Cubans, a Quebecoise snowbird named Chantal, and Karen, the American Chantal.

Chantal is from Gatineau. Karen is her American equivalent. Karen has never lost a fight with a manager. Karen knows the HOA president personally. You learn things from Karen that business school charges six figures for.

Half the street left New York in the last six years. They were Democrats when they packed. The property taxes converted them somewhere on I-95. They drive German cars, vote red, and complain about the price of everything except their own houses.

You're between two worlds again. On one side, Latinos who own landscaping companies and send money home. On the other, rich boomers who read Zillow like scripture. Politics comes up once, at Karen's pool. You say you don't really follow it. The table goes quiet. Someone hands you a beer. Nobody ever asks again.

The fief: the villa, the trucks, the company, the accounts, a generator, forty days of water, a lawyer on retainer. The good conscience is the villa. The stronghold is everything else.

You hear about the street from time to time. It's not the same street.

Deb got carjacked at a gas station in 2025. Two guys. Sudanese - the kind Minneapolis sent two thousand federal agents about. They took the Prius and her phone. She posted about the event. She posted about the systemic causes. She posted carefully. Not about the men.

Six months later they were back. Not the same two. The cousin of one of them, maybe. Nobody knows. What's known: Deb's back door doesn't close the way it used to, and a man named Ahmed sleeps in the living room now. It's not a lease. It's not a sale. Deb calls it a complicated housing situation. The city calls it nothing.

The neighborhood went down the way they do. One house, then a block party with a shooting, then a for-sale sign that never sold, then tents. There's no year it turned. It turned.

Deb fell into the tranq dope. Fentanyl cut with a horse sedative. Then a newer one, when the first got famous: medetomidine. It's for dogs after surgery. It's not for people. The people it doesn't kill, it freezes. They stand hunched on lawns, swaying, mid-gesture, for hours. The internet calls them zombies. Deb called it a failure of compassion until one of them was her.

Rick woke up. Rick read the files that exist. Trump backed Israel. The wall stayed a wall of the mind. The Epstein files stayed filed. The wars went on - for the complex, the lobbies, the things Rick now explains at length, in his bunker. The bunker is real: forty feet of shipping container under the garden, ventilation, water, ammo, freeze-dried beef, a flag, a Bible. He built it in 2025.

Rick's house stands empty above the bunker. The statues moved in. That's what you call them. Tranq doesn't make people lie down. It makes them stand frozen, leaning, swaying, holding a pose. There are four of them in Rick's living room. The house is lost. The bunker is his. The statues can have the surface. He's going to save America from below.

You go back once, for your mother's funeral. You park the truck between Deb's squat and Rick's statue garden. Two flags on one street: a Pride flag nobody took down, an American flag nobody took in. At the wake, people ask about Florida. You say the taxes are low. They look at you the way they look at the weather.

A cousin asks if you're coming back. Ahmed's friends are moving a couch into Deb's house. A statue stands in Rick's flowerbed, swaying, holding a phone. The kid next door asks the statue if he's okay. The statue says he's good. Nobody laughs. The street is very quiet and very loud.

You fly back the same night, first class, on points. In Florida it's 78 degrees. Chantal is playing pickleball. Karen is suing the HOA. The villa is lit, the generator is full, the company runs without you. The phone rings with another data center.

You practice americanmaxxing. It's not a team. It's the thing the street forgot: move forward, keep the fief, never argue with a statue. Deb practices democratmaxxing. Rick practices trumpmaxxing. The street practices both for them. You've practiced yours since you were born. Now you know what it's called.

Some people have turned their brains into toilets for political garbage. What a shameful waste of intelligence!

There is a bird called a vulture. It feeds on dead, rotten and decaying flesh. It does not spend its day hunting healthy animals. It circles the skies, patiently waiting for something to die so it can descend and feast on the carcass. It is nature's garbage collector.

Unfortunately, some of our brilliant Luo minds have reduced themselves to political vultures.

Educated, articulate people with enormous intellectual potential, yet their entire political existence revolves around waiting for somebody to fall, celebrating another person's misfortune, manufacturing hatred and scavenging on political disagreements.

They cannot formulate an idea. They cannot build a movement. They cannot organise people around development. They cannot inspire the next generation. Their only political currency is somebody else's downfall.

They wake up looking for political carcasses. When a leader makes a mistake, they descend. When a political alliance experiences disagreement, they feast. When somebody loses an opportunity, they celebrate as though their own lives have suddenly improved.

Imagine having a brilliant brain but choosing to operate like a scavenger!

The tragedy is not that Luo land lacks intellectual capacity. The tragedy is that some of its brightest minds have surrendered their intelligence to jealousy, negative competition, political prostitution and the desperate need to see others fail.

You cannot build your future by feeding on somebody else's misfortunes. You cannot become relevant by wishing everybody else irrelevant.

Luo land needs intellectual warriors, not political vultures. We need people who can challenge ideas, build institutions, create opportunities and offer solutions.

Stop circling other people's political carcasses. Develop your own wings and learn to fly!

The community needs builders, not professional scavengers.

Does thinking he'll be treated like that make him leave?

Nuggets owners also showed incompetence with the Malone-Booth feud and more. Can he trust them?

If he at least looks around: what teams seem realistic?

Jokic and Luka are good friends who joke around at All Star games and Jokic age 31 only has one late prime.

Brave AI on Lakers 2027 cap space:

"Despite being over the cap, they are projected to have approximately $43.4 million in space under the second apron (hard cap at ~$222 million)."

Jokic should thank Nuggets fans for many good years and say he wants to have fun with his friend Luka.

Jokic is too old and slow to protect the rim. But, Kessler helps and Jokic can shoot and pass at power forward.

Luka, Austin, Jake, Zaire or an upgrade, Jokic, Kessler.

They may be incredibly fun on offense getting creative.

But, maybe flammable enough on defence to beat them.

So, it's not a "KD to the Warriors" thing, though it's close.

If the Lakers have $43 million in cap space now they can probably make more. Jokic can ask for a sign and trade so the Nuggets get back something and sign a team friendly deal like many stars now do, like Wemby taking $50 million a year or 25% of the cap instead of 30%.

Jokic could make more money off court to recoup the difference. Despite talk of him being reclusive and only liking horses? He has a shoe deal, does commericials, and doesn't seem to be scared of the attention the Lakers bring and may enjoy it and the great weather.

The only thing the Nuggets have to offer is big, but still.

Brave AI:

"Jokic’s decision to delay extension talks is strategically motivated by the potential to secure a five-year, $359.5 million contract as a free agent, which would be the largest in NBA history and increase his career earnings to approximately $724 million."

Is it worth leaving maybe $100 million in guaranteed NBA money to leave the fading Nuggets for a better chance to win another ring with the rising Lakers and rising star and good friend Luka? Recoup money with commercials and connections? Enjoy it more?

Brave AI:

"Nikola Jokić has spent his entire 12-season NBA career with the Denver Nuggets, having been selected in the second round (11th pick, 41st overall) of the 2014 NBA Draft."

Seems like the Nuggets had a great run that's run its course with no ways to get consistently good athletes and defenders to contend with Jokic who's neither.

So, they can sell off their aging vets, rebuild with the picks they get and look for their next franchise star. 

I feel bad for Nuggets fans. But, like KG in Minnesota? Sometimes you give it your all then give it a rest.

Would Nuggets fans like to see Jokic go out like Dirk? Wasting away on mid teams but still nice to have?

Or, to get stuff back from trading him, wish him well, then enjoy Jokic, Luka and Austin making magic?

People can decide for themselves what they want and what would make for better basketball to enjoy.

text:
Ioannia - Greece

In northwestern Greece, surrounded by mountains and built beside a beautiful lake, Ioannina has a personality that is quite different from the country's better-known coastal destinations. It is atmospheric, historic and full of little discoveries, with a relaxed pace that makes it easy to fall in love with.

Lake Pamvotida is at the heart of the city. Its waterfront promenade is a favourite place for a walk, while the changing light across the water gives Ioannina a special charm throughout the day. In cooler months, mist sometimes settles over the lake, creating an almost mysterious atmosphere.

One of the most memorable experiences is taking a small boat across to the island of Ioannina. Despite its modest size, the island has traditional lanes, monasteries, small museums and waterfront tavernas serving local dishes.

Here are some experiences not to miss:
•  Explore Ioannina Castle: Wander through its historic quarters, discover museums and enjoy views from the old fortifications.
•  Take a boat to the island: Explore its traditional settlements, monasteries and peaceful lakeside paths.
•  Walk beside Lake Pamvotida: Enjoy the scenery, watch the boats and stop at one of the cafés along the waterfront.
•  Discover the city's history: Visit the museums and historic buildings that tell the story of Ioannina's diverse past.
•  Try the local cuisine: Look out for traditional pies, local cheeses, grilled meats and dishes featuring lake fish.

Ioannina is also known for its silversmithing tradition. Around the old town, you can find shops displaying beautifully crafted silver jewellery and decorative objects, a reminder of an important local art that has been passed down through generations.

Food is another reason to linger. The region of Epirus is famous for its pies, and a visit offers plenty of opportunities to sample local recipes alongside traditional Greek dishes.

With Zagori, the Vikos Gorge and the wider landscapes of Epirus within reach, Ioannina also makes an excellent base for exploring the region. It is a destination that offers far more than a quick stop, and one that rewards visitors who take the time to look beyond the obvious.

text:
I’ve seen plenty of criticism directed at Isaiah Glasker the last few weeks, including people calling for him to be benched. I just want to take a minute and give some perspective on what I’m seeing on film and what this guy has done at BYU.

Isaiah came out of Bingham with two scholarship offers. BYU and Weber State. He came to Provo as a safety and turned himself into one of the best linebackers in BYU history.

Here’s a favorite stat....

Only four players in BYU history have recorded at least 24 tackles for loss and five interceptions. Kyle Van Noy, Fred Warner, Cameron Jensen and Isaiah Glasker.

Through the Utah game, No. 16 has 175 tackles, 24 tackles for loss, 8 sacks, 9 pass breakups and 5 picks, including a pick-six. Among BYU linebackers, he’s 12th in tackles for loss and tied for 10th in interceptions. He was the 2024 Alamo Bowl Defensive MVP after putting up eight tackles and a pick against Colorado.

He got hurt last season in the Colorado game and didn't get back to form.. This season he got hurt against TCU, missed Iowa State and came back with six tackles and three pass breakups in a win over No. 2 Notre Dame. I thought it was one of the best games he’s played at BYU.

My understanding is he’s been dealing multiple lower extremity injuries..

 For a guy with his length at 6-foot-5, Isaiah has always played with a strong base. You can still see that elite closing speed on film. Where I’ve noticed him struggle on some reps is in deceleration. You’ve got to decelerate, sink your hips, come to balance and absorb contact while the ball carrier is trying to make you miss. 

 He's also fought through stinger issues that are probably contributing to is lack of wrapping up. 

He’s still making big-time plays. Go watch that Notre Dame game again. Coming back and playing at that level is a credit to his grit, his toughness and how good a football player he is. Hopefully he can get back to 100% in the last few games. They'll need him to play at his best.

text:
🚨 Let me point out a few things about one of the biggest plays in this game, and elements that aren’t getting enough attention 🚨 

3rd Quarter | 3:31 remaining
BYU 20 – Utah 14
3rd & 7 from the BYU 21

BYU shows a simulated five man pressure but only brings four. Getting home in 1.5 second with a 4 man rush and 7 in coverage is ELITE DEFENSIVE PLAY. 

1. BYU DID USE A QB SPY‼️

I’ve heard plenty of BYU fans complaining that the Cougars never assigned a spy to Devon Dampier.

Watch Cade Uluave on this play. He’s spying Dampier in the middle of the field but loses sight of him and takes the wrong pursuit angle as he closes toward the line of scrimmage.

The spy was there. The execution wasn’t.

2. ELITE PLAY, BUT DOESN’T FINISH THE TACKLE.
WHY❓

Very few defenders can beat a Power Four offensive guard the way Isaiah Glasker does here.

His inside swim move is elite. He wins immediately at the LOS and puts himself in position to make a tackle for loss.

But he doesn’t finish the play.

It’s fair to criticize the missed tackle, but don’t overlook the exceptional individual effort it took to get there in the first place.

3. THE PHYSICAL MATCHUP AND INJURY HISTORY MATTER.

Devon Dampier is listed at 5’10”, 210 pounds. That’s a compact, powerful runner with a low center of gravity, tremendous balance and strength.

Glasker is approximately 6’4½” and suffered a lower-leg injury against TCU. He hasn’t appeared to be at full strength since.

At that height, getting low enough to wrap up a shorter, powerful quarterback is already challenging. A lower-leg injury could further compromise his ability to bend, balance, change direction and finish tackles.

Something else I’ve noticed: Glasker has struggled to consistently wrap up and finish tackles recently. I wonder how much of that is related to the lower-leg injury, And history of stingers 

Dealing with stingers throughout his career, he wears a cowboy collar for additional neck/shoulder support. Could that history be contributing to some hesitation or difficulty getting into ideal tackling position? It’s worth considering

I’m not making excuses for missed tackles. I’m looking at the physical factors that could explain why an otherwise exceptional NFL caliber defender is struggling to finish plays.

📋 In summary 📋

Great play call on 3rd and 7. You had pressure and coverage. BYU had a spy. Glasker beat his blocker. The defense had an opportunity to make a tackle behind the line of scrimmage.

The defensive design put players in position to make a play. They simply didn’t finish.

There’s a difference between poor defensive design and poor execution.

And sometimes, you have to give credit to the opposing quarterback for making a great play.

But Forcing a FG here may have changed the outcome of the game.  https://t.co/UlJsu9EO97

text:
The Discipline No One Assigns

Every autumn, a new cohort arrives at university armed with the habits that earned them admission: punctuality, obedience to a syllabus, a practised facility for examinations. Within months, many find these habits oddly insufficient. The timetable thins; the supervision recedes; the hours, once rationed by others, are suddenly their own. This is usually called freedom. It is more accurately a test, and what it tests is the capacity that secondary education, for all its rigour, rarely cultivates: the capacity to direct one's own learning.
That this capacity matters more than any other is not self-evident. Universities are asked to produce many things: technical competence, critical judgment, eloquence, resilience, the ability to work with others. None is dispensable. Yet each depends, to a degree seldom acknowledged, on a prior habit. Critical judgment is not conferred by lectures alone; it develops when students question, test, and extend what they are taught. Eloquence owes much to a tutor's corrections, yet corrections instruct only those who return to the page of their own accord. Self-direction is not the sole source of these virtues; it is the condition under which they mature rather than stall.
The fate of knowledge itself strengthens the case. Seldom has the half-life of professional expertise been so short. Standards are revised, technologies superseded, and routine work quietly absorbed by machines, so that a graduate who has merely mastered the curriculum of the day holds an asset already depreciating. What does not depreciate is the ability to acquire the next body of knowledge unaided. It is this ability, rather than any particular stock of facts, that a degree ought to certify.
Why, then, do so many students fail to develop it? The explanation lies less in indolence than in conditioning. For twelve years, the typical student has been told what to learn, when to learn it, and how success will be measured. Small wonder that, when the scaffolding is withdrawn, the structure it supported should wobble. The drift so common among first-year students is not a moral failing. It is the predictable consequence of asking people to exercise a muscle they were never invited to use.
None of this absolves the student. Institutions can mitigate the difficulty; they cannot remove it. Consider a student of accounting who, having completed an exercise on depreciation, remains uneasy about why two permitted methods should yield different profits. The assignment is finished; the question is not. She consults the standard itself, discovers that she had misread her textbook, and takes her corrected reasoning to a lecturer to be tested. None of this was required. Yet it contains the whole of the matter: a gap noticed, a source weighed, an error owned, and help sought not as a substitute for effort but as its completion.
Such habits are unglamorous. They are also cumulative, and over four years they do much to distinguish those who leave university educated from those who leave it merely credentialed. Nor do they imply any disdain for instruction. The self-directed learner uses teachers and curricula deliberately rather than passively, as a traveller uses a map rather than as a passenger uses a train.
University offers knowledge to all who enrol, but an education only to those prepared to claim it. Instruction is given; learning is taken. The student who grasps this early will find the bewildering liberty of the first year neither a holiday nor a void, but an apprenticeship in the one discipline that no one else can assign.

text:
The potato has spent 450 years as the food rulers hand to people they cannot be bothered to feed properly, and now it is being sold back to you as a superfood.

1570s. The Spanish silver mines at Potosí run on forced Indigenous labour, and the men hauling ore up through the mountain are kept going on chuño, potatoes freeze-dried in the Andean night. The silver sails to Madrid. The potato stays down the mine.

1756. Frederick the Great issues his Potato Order, because an acre of potatoes keeps more peasants and soldiers alive than an acre of grain. Nobody asks the peasants what they would like for dinner.

1772. A French academy offers a prize for the best food to carry the poor through a famine. Antoine Parmentier wins it with the potato, which he first ate as a prisoner of war, because that is what the Prussians fed their prisoners.

1795. Count Rumford, running the workhouses of Munich, calculates the cheapest soup that will keep a pauper upright, barley, peas, potatoes and stale bread boiled in vinegared water, and soup kitchens across Europe ladle it out for a century.

1845. A third of Ireland lives almost entirely on one variety, the Lumper, chosen because it cropped on the worst ground a landlord could rent out. Every plant is a clone of the next, the blight takes the lot in a season, and a million people die.

1941. Lord Woolton rations the bacon, the butter, the meat and the cheese, and leaves the potato free for the entire war. The Savoy names a pie after him, potato and swede under a lid of more potato, and a cartoon called Potato Pete is sent out to sing at the nation.

1974. Smash fills British televisions with metal Martians laughing at humans for peeling potatoes, and a country that once ate dripping by the tin starts eating potato dust from a packet.

1998. After a famine that killed hundreds of thousands, Kim Jong Il declares a potato revolution and orders North Korea to plant them.

2008. The United Nations declares the International Year of the Potato as its answer to world hunger.

2015. China launches a national drive to make the potato its fourth staple alongside rice, wheat and maize, and starts pushing potato noodles and potato bread at a population that would rather have pork.

2026. A man with a ring light eats nothing but boiled potatoes for a month, films every weigh-in, and calls it a superfood.

Mine owners, kings, workhouse masters, ministers of food and dictators all reached for the potato, and every one of them was serving it to somebody else.

It has always been the food that is handed down, never the food that is chosen. The only new thing about it is the ring light.

Because you are lazy let me help you. A simple google map search will show you the neighborhoods and houses around it and is on both sides of the Stateline Rd W. Don’t be lazy. 

And a simple further google search will tell you the following- Yes, Elon Musk’s data center campus—operating under the SpaceXAI / xAI name—sits directly adjacent to several historic, long-established residential neighborhoods. Because the corporate campus stretches right across the Tennessee-Mississippi state line, it impacts communities in both southwest Memphis and northern Southaven.
The main neighborhoods directly bordering the data centers include:
•Whitehaven (Memphis, TN): This historic, predominantly Black neighborhood in southwest Memphis surrounds the northern side of the expansion. The Colossus 2 facility sits right within this area on Tulane Road.
•Colonial Hills (Southaven, MS):Located just south of the state line, this residential neighborhood sits right next to the incoming "Gun Range" and "Spam" data center sites.
•Boxtown (South Memphis, TN):Situated slightly further west near the original Colossus 1 data center on Riverport Road, this historic neighborhood has been a focal point for community concerns.
Community Impact & Displacements
The rapid, nonstop construction of the supercomputer cluster has triggered significant local friction.
•Property Buyouts and Rental Evictions: In neighborhoods like Colonial Hills, the expansion is actively altering the residential landscape. An affiliate of the tech company has purchased homes in the area, leading to situations where some homeowners received buyout offers while renters were asked to vacate because their landlords sold the properties.
•Noise and Traffic: Local residents frequently raise concerns over the constant whirring noise from the massive gas turbines used to power the facilities, alongside heavy construction traffic moving through neighborhood streets.
•Environmental Moratoriums: The proximity to these neighborhoods has led to intense debates at City Hall. Residents and local advocates recently pushed for strict oversight, resulting in the Memphis City Council voting for a 135-day pause on new data center developments to evaluate air quality and community impacts.

￼
The physical footprint of the xAI data center campus has significantly altered the environment across Southwest Memphis and Southaven. Because the facility was built at unprecedented speed, researchers have heavily relied on NASA and NOAA satellite instruments to track the "before and after" shifts in air quality and land use.
The Air Quality Shift: Before vs. After
Because Southwest Memphis lacked a dense network of ground-level air monitoring stations, scientists from the University of Memphis and independent research groups used space-based data to measure the changes.
•Before xAI: The industrial corridor of Southwest Memphis was already heavily burdened by emissions from regional logistics hubs, an oil refinery, and a steel mill. However, the specific pocket near Boxtown maintained a baseline of localized industrial emissions.
•After xAI: The activation of dozens of massive, trailer-mounted methane gas turbines to power the supercomputers drastically altered the local atmosphere. Data captured by NASA's TEMPO satellite instrument revealed that peak nitrogen dioxide () concentration levels spiked by 79%in the immediate vicinity of the campus compared to pre-xAI levels.
The primary driver of this atmospheric degradation is the massive release of smog-forming nitrogen oxides () and formaldehydes from the site, making the tech campus one of the single largest industrial sources of smog in Shelby County.
The Landscape Transformation from Space
Satellite timelapses and aerial mapping showcase a rapid, stark transition from residential and light-industrial utility to high-density power generation:

text:
ONE DAY A MADMAN WILL COME AND I’LL GET SHOT DOWN ON STAGE (Looking back at the contradictions of the typical, free-riding anarchist singer three years after May 1968, caught between the power he refuses but whose protection he enjoys, the attempts at recuperation by the socialist left embodied by the socialist deputy and mayor of Marseille Gaston Defferre and the violent contestations by leftist groupuscules who reproached him for his commercial success and money)

Léo Ferré is still pretending to believe in Santa Claus. One has to remain a child to believe in the best of all possible worlds, where power would be abolished.

Pierre Goldman (1978)

https://t.co/Fr1AAa1J1o

I urge, then, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercession and thanksgiving be made for all people—for kings and all those in authority, that we may live peaceful and quiet lives in all godliness and holiness.

First Letter of Paul to Timothy 2:1-2

Let everyone be subject to the governing authorities… For rulers hold no terror for those who do right, but for those who do wrong. Do you want to be free from fear of the one in authority? Then do what is right and you will be commended. For the one in authority is God’s servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for rulers do not bear the sword for no reason. They are God’s servants, agents of wrath to bring punishment on the wrongdoer… This is also why you pay taxes, for the authorities are God’s servants, who give their full time to governing. Give to everyone what you owe them: If you owe taxes, pay taxes; if revenue, then revenue; if respect, then respect; if honour, then honour.

Paul (Letter to the Romans 13:1-7)

Those who are disadvantaged by the prohibition of acts that would only risk harming others must be compensated for these disadvantages imposed upon them in order to ensure the security of others. But would this compensation mechanism not create another free-rider problem? Not to a great extent, since compensation is paid only to those who would be disadvantaged if they had to buy protection themselves, and only to the extent corresponding to the cost of an unfancy police force, added to the sum of the monetary costs of self-defence protection plus the amount the person could comfortably pay. Moreover, the agency protects these independents whom it compensates only against its own paying clients, upon whom the independents are forbidden to exercise self-enforcement of their rights. The more free-riders there are, the more desirable it is to be a client always protected by the agency. This factor, with the others, contributes to reducing the number of free-riders and tending the equilibrium toward near-universal participation. (…) the dominant protective agency on a territory satisfied two crucial necessary conditions for being a State: that it possess the type of monopoly required on the use of force in that territory, and that it protect the rights of everyone on that territory, even if this universal protection could be assured only in a “redistributive” manner. These very crucial aspects of the State constituted precisely the object of the condemnation of the State as immoral by the individualist anarchists. [As we have shown] these elements of monopoly and redistribution [are] themselves morally legitimate, that is to say that the passage from a state of nature to an ultra-minimal State (the monopoly element) [is] morally legitimate and does not [violate] anyone’s rights, and (…) the passage from an ultra-minimal State to a minimal State (the “redistributive” element) [is] equally morally legitimate and does not [violate] anyone’s rights.

Robert Nozick (Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974)

https://t.co/EagOQi3TCu

I have chosen to take as my masters freedom, anarchy. I live in hotels, at the mercy of the tours, surrounded by young people. May 68 is more important than 89. Every year I sang there for the anarchists’ gala; this time I will do Léo Ferré, whose myth must be destroyed. Stars are washing machines. (…) I am a provocateur, I violate the thinking of those who refuse to think and, if I often use crude words like “arse”, it is because a real woman is capable of understanding the meaning. When I was a child, to make me sing dirty songs, they gave me liquorice. I have always been bought so that I would sing. But when I sell myself, I don’t know who is taking me. (…) Sometimes I get attacked when I sing, it disarms me. The stage is the only domain where one can express oneself in freedom. One day a madman will come and I’ll get shot down on stage.

Léo Ferré (France Soir, 06/01/1971)

By showing our ideas, we show ourselves. The writer or the journalist gives his paper to the marble and the public does not see him. But the singer expresses ideas directly, and they can shock people. From that moment, they are no longer the ideas of Léo Ferré but those of the guy dressed in black, in front of the people, and he has to fight. (…) I am against right-wing people, not against the “gauchistes”. This word is an appellation made public by the Communist Party. I did write a song for La Cause du peuple, even though I do not share their ideas. But freedom of the press is an essential thing for me, and I like Politique Hebdo. I find it a well-made paper. At one time I preached disengagement, but today that is no longer possible. In Mulhouse there is a Peugeot worker who has been laid off and can no longer find work; I am going to sing on Saturday at a gala for him. (…) A worker, when I see his hands, when I imagine him working in precise conditions, well! I am ashamed of the life I lead. The guy from Mulhouse asked me to do something for him; I was not free that day, but I told him I would come back as soon as possible. That said, that is not why tomorrow I am going to do political tours or join a party, which remains contrary to my position. (…) [Discussions with workers and the public in general] No longer. Before, yes, but it often ended badly. There were always one or two guys who came to shout at me. So now, at the end of the recital, I go out immediately and I am in the street with the people. (…) When you plant seeds, sometimes it grows, sometimes not. I believe that ideas sent like that into people’s heads, with the help of music which is a great violator of consciences, end up getting in. I often notice it from the mail I receive; and the people who repeat that in any case nothing changes, so “no point in acting”, there are many of them and it is despairing. (…) [Singing in the open air or in the street] First of all, in the street I do not have the right. I would have to take a hawker’s licence. And then, don’t you think there are enough spectacles in the street? When I was a kid, coming out of the cinema, I was sad resuming contact with everyday reality. Art is an elegant lie: it makes the rest pass. (…) [On the future of the political situation in France] I am very pessimistic. One would have to look in America, where many people say that it is they who are going to make the revolution. In France, it is the last bourgeois country that will defend itself. It is a country where the bourgeois kill. Here, the structures are made so that people are docile. One day someone posed the problem of money to Brassens; he had a very good answer: “When people pay to see us, they pay, we cheat no one and it is a gift they make us.” On the other hand, put Messrs Pompidou, Nixon, Agnelli (the boss of Fiat in Italy) and say to them: “Earn money with what you do yourselves, and not with the work of others.” Well! they die. We live with our work, what we have written. And I, my author’s rights come back and then they are used again by this same society. People are disciplined in the cities because they are in perpetual danger; if you like, it is conditioning; it is not only Pavlov who conditioned the dogs. We are all dogs, in fact; I, when I see a pretty girl who pleases me, my mouth waters. Isn’t that conditioning? (…) [Going down into the street to fight if there were a revolution in France] Yes, it seems to me that there would be no question, because I am a man (apart from the technique: one has to learn to throw paving stones). No, I would probably be afraid, but I would do it all the same.

Léo Ferré (1971)

https://t.co/1gQcEKe4LD

In France, pop equals helmets, truncheons, cops, iron bars, riot, repression, free concerts. (…) Since May 1968, the youth movement is severely repressed, militants locked up, political actions broken or necessarily secret. Outside the factory or work, youth has only one common meeting place that is proper to it: the pop concert. It alone offers a wide tribune to underlying ideas, to suppressed ideologies, to shared questions. A good reason to ban them, limit the number of participants, try to contain the phenomenon within groupuscule limits. / Yet, through the music and its gatherings, ideological exchange takes place, a culture forms, “demonstrations” articulate themselves; the concert is for the moment one of the only possible places.

Actuel (Free, pop and politics, 1971)

Cops everywhere, helmeted, armed to the teeth, terribly threatening. Millions of cops. And endless provocations, insults and threats to the poor young people trying to get in to listen to music, their music. The young people, almost children, are calm and do not reply to the insults. While the cops, mad with rage, hit them with their truncheons and massacre them. There, that is how it should have happened for things to be simple and logic respected. It was, strangely, the exact opposite. Nothing that evening happened as usual, and afterwards neither. […] Everything happened the wrong way round. There were only about twenty skinny cops in capes in front of the doors, and the shock, sudden, violent, made them fly into pieces. Young people—very young—rushed at them with iron bars, pulverised them with incredible rage then smashed the doors to get in. Stunned and bloody, the police hastened to call for reinforcements. (…) Young people, iron bars and bottle shards in hand, circled around the English musicians who were not looking too confident. What they wanted exactly is hard to know. Others continued their exploration, visiting every corner of the immense building, breaking here and there a little thing or a little guy who resisted them too much. (…) Near the stage, some types systematically smashed seats with crowbars. They stopped, danced, applauded then started again, stubborn. (…) Then it was the party, against a background of unease and fear (…) when the food reserves of the Palais des Sports suddenly poured down on heads for an hour. It began with bread, armfuls of baguettes flying in the air, then there were thousands of ice creams, so many one could choose one’s flavour, pâté, sausage, cognac, billions of sweets and chewing-gum, even champagne. […] the crowd […] had become complicit. Beer. Fruit juice. In abundance.

Philippe Paringaux (Rock & Folk, March 1971)

We are all ashamed to be French. On one side, open provocation, excessive politicisation, vandalism, stupidity. / On the other, silent provocation, the easy grenade, the truncheon even more, blind savagery, stupidity. Human stupidity… One always comes back to it. (…) we were there, all of us, at the Palais des Sports, hungry for music, the one that makes the guts beat to its rhythm. We are still hungry, still… because of us, stupid French. Disgusted.

Reader (Actuel, 1971)

Your little gauchiste darlings have once again devastated the Palais des Sports. Pop music is left-wing, declare Alessandrini and his clique.

Reader

Float a bit, get stoned, shoot up, send yourselves into the air, whatever, and stop breaking our planets with your political hall. You saw what the mixture gives and gave at the Palais des Sports. OK, we had fun but now, music: finished.

Reader

This link [between gauchisme and music] is also made by the government, which explains the bans on festivals (any gathering of young people is dangerous) and also the incidents that opposed the forces of order last May to the young people queuing at the Celtic cinema to see Amougies.

Philippe Aubert (L’agit-pop, Actuel, August 1971)

I no longer want to have to dread the fights that risk degenerating into catastrophe.

Jean-Michel Boris (assistant to Bruno Coquatrix, director of the Olympia, Rock & Folk, July 1971)

I am a bit disappointed by the public. Me, calling the police now does not amuse me at all, but I am obliged to by a certain number of people who take us for exploiters whereas we are exploited by the groups. (…) there is gate-crashing, I have seen it at all times; (…) but then, to politicise the problem and pass to violence, then I no longer agree. (..) [After the Santana concert at the Olympia, which degenerated] I prefer to stop rather than end up at the Palais des Sports. (... [The beginnings of Johnny Hallyday] it was different. (…) there were the heavies (…), but they paid their place, they tried to be as close as possible to the artist, but they did not politicise the thing. (...) thirty-eight years old, well, at each Musicorama I come out a bit more exhausted nervously and physically. Listen, I recognise it, I am scared, but I do not want to die at forty. Each time now I have the impression of brushing against catastrophe. It is not possible. If the young people had this self-discipline, if they organised themselves, it would be wonderful… but there, now, there is this tension, it is unbearable, my heart is hurting me, really hurting… I will admit to you that very selfishly, it is perhaps that which now most inclines me to drop it. I admit that I lack courage. (...) These gate-crashers, three hundred of them, seize the front rows, and (…) remove those who have paid. Then those who have paid defend themselves. (…] Then it is the fight.

Jean-Michel Boris (Rock & Folk, July 1971)

The pop musician is far from constituting an exemplary militant. The prospect of getting up early and distributing a tract does not fill him with enthusiasm. (...) One of the obstacles to this synthesis between musical revolt and political revolt (…) is apathy, tranquillity, dream, escape through pop music. Following the old popular saying “While they are listening to that, they are not thinking of throwing paving stones”. It is partly true. Pop festivals are, for many adults, reassuring. The young people are calm there, among themselves, outside the old world and consequently they are not dangerous for this world. It is true that one listens to a certain number of groups, but that becomes false when these groups are politicised. Of course, spending an hour in the company of the Bee-Gees has never incited anyone to launch a strike. On the contrary, even. A certain form of pop music is as much like marshmallow as ointment. The music is syrupy, the listener put to sleep. The number of groups one can assimilate to this somniferous tendency is alas important. The Beatles themselves are not strangers to it. But after having listened to Country Joe, Richie Havens, the Rolling Stones, Jefferson Airplane and many others, the public is forced to feel different: it loves the music that breaks the usual criteria, it enters “the margin”.

Philippe Aubert (Actuel, no 6, March 1971)

Would pop be becoming “calming”.

Paris-Normandie (1971)

How to resist? Soon the hyper-excited fans assault the stage. It is the inevitable fight that everything predicted. The mic stands become formidable clubs in the hands of the besieged. Near me, a boy who has lost his mind, bursts four bulbs of a torn garland with headbutts. Electric cables are cut with a knife. The projector bases fly while a spotlight is reduced to pieces in a grenade noise: Suddenly everything becomes blurred, degrading until I discover a little boy of seven or eight lost in this turmoil. On the edge of the “stage-ring”, his face resting on his folded arms, he fixes me with a look of strange intensity: “it was beautiful, Monsieur, it was beautiful”. For him, no doubt, for half an hour the horseman of his illustrated albums took him on the croup… But what is this kid in the yellow sweater doing here this evening? […] Johnny’s passage at Le Havre will have been marked by twenty wounded.

Pierre Joly (Twenty encores… No, twenty wounded: Johnny Hallyday’s Le Havre recital, Paris-Normandie, 1970)

He has not changed. Spokesman of a whole generation in search of escape, he has reigned over his subjects for fifteen years. And nothing calls his power into question. His fans of 1960 have aged. They have swapped the vinyl jacket for the leather jacket with fur collar or the classic overcoat. But they have not forgotten him. What is more, they have brought behind them a horde of young people who find in the Claude François genre not the slightest suspicion of aggressiveness or disobedience. Johnny, he is the incarnation of refusal, of revolt. Constantly, his origins, his desire to fight against life come back in his refrains. He is alone, he is desperate, he needs to be loved. Johnny the hard, the violent, is also Johnny the weak and the solitary. He sings it. He shouts it. He finds 5,000 people in communion with him. They are there to see him. Or rather to “have seen him”. One does not have the right to miss a Hallyday show. Is it not said moreover that it is one of the last shows of the king annoyed at paying so many taxes that he prefers exile.

Bernadette Poulain (Johnny Hallyday tonight at the Parc-Expo, Paris-Normandie, 14 December 1976)

“The working class will not work with a pistol in its back”, the paper adds. The victim is shot while distributing tracts denouncing crimes perpetrated on “dozens of Arab workers […] found dead, several openly assassinated by racists. And that in indifference and silence.”

La Cause du peuple (Halt to fascism!, after the death on 25 February at Boulogne-Billancourt of Pierre Overney, Maoist militant, February 1972)

We will not change the world by democratic ways, there will be violence, I hate, I hate, I hate, I hate violence because it terrifies me, we will have to fight with our red blood, red like blood.

Catherine Ribeiro (1974)

This “state of violence” largely overflows the usual theatre of demonstrations, since it invites itself jointly into the enclosure of southern Pop festivals or into a few Parisian concerts. The example of the mad night at the Palais des Sports on 31 January 1971, which promised a fine bill for young fans of Pop Music, underlines this contestatory and sometimes politicised shift onto the rock stage. The violence of the smashers and gate-crashers, if it finally involves only a few hundred young people and concerns very few concerts, will have the consequence of slowing the development of a new youth culture, as shown by the testimony of Jean-Michel Boris forced to abandon pop concerts at the Olympia. The public authorities and organisers thus try to contain the enthusiasm for what France calls “Pop Music”, a new progressive music which in fact will produce only a soothing effect on the young public rather than encouraging it to engage in the struggle. This contradiction does not escape the journalists, for, as observers of these sometimes decadent and noisy concerts, they multiply the testimonies on this apathetic and cerebral public attending the performances of Soft Machine, Julie Driscoll or Martin Circus. Pop Music would therefore be calming the youth of the 1970s to such an extent that groups like Deep Purple preferred to cut short their hexagonal tour, tired of the indifference of the French public. To this youth is opposed at the same period a working-class youth, fiery, aggressive or revolted, which frequents the concerts of Johnny Hallyday where tumult is always on the agenda. The “rockers” are framed by an impressive security organisation to protect the idol, “explosive social phenomenon”, recognised by the press as a particular case.

Joann Élart (Violence and non-violence in rock concerts or 1970s French society facing its contradictions, 2018)

https://t.co/JXbwTjplpK

When one sees in France for example the people who call themselves left-wing (…) The left is a waiting room for fascism. Yes indeed! The examples are there everywhere. To all the people, all the politicians, the characters who call themselves left-wing who one day arrive in power… there are too many idiots. Do you know the left-wing artist in what he does? No no, in the technique… No no, in his paper and his pen, that is what I mean. And one day a deputy [inaudible name] with whom I was at dinner, then deputy friends, is called… who said to me without laughing at one moment: “the law is the authority of the law”. I really wanted to spit in his face. This guy, I finally saw in front of me… what was curious is that I saw an elected of the people… He was eating his foie gras well, quiet in his chair, perfect, the tie thing… the bourgeoisie up to the edges of the eyes, you understand? These people who call themselves left-wing, that is what is killing this country. There is no journalist here? No… With you? there is no perfect journalism. Because I see no more… it is finished, I see no more journalists. They do too much harm. It is true. Roughly, in general what… Mean…

Léo Ferré (1971)

text:
So many black girls in my life are so upset. 

I never heard this much talk of "colonizers" and this much anti-white anger. 

I get it. 
I grew up in West Virginia.
Seeing Confederate flags nearly every day.
Being called a nigger to my face - sometimes by friends, jokingly...which only made it worse.

I wasn't allowed to date my high school girlfriend because I was black (imagine THAT was the reason when there were a MILLION others). 

I've been pulled over by racist cops.
I know better than to be at certain places at night. 

Mind you, I love and adore rednecks - and I know the difference between provincial innocence and genuine "racism". 

I also know that white people are probably the most accommodating people...to the point of suicidal cultural empathy. 

And yet, there really are systemic issues that most white people do not intend. 

And yes, white people are met with unfair double standards...and yet, white people really do occupy a unique position in the current paradigm of order that may seemingly justify those double standards DESPITE the fact that, yes, white people, too, suffer from systemic issues, and despite that, yes, it really is unfair that people today should have to inherit the sins of the past. 

And there's a reason that the whole cultural conversation is stuck at an impasse - things I won't get into here. 

But I will offer something brief. 

No human architected the original conditions of existence. 
The fact that we have to eat.
The fact that resources are scarce...etc

And - assuming that we share a "human nature" - groups (based on metaphysical accident) acted with regard to their self-interest (if you want to put an evo psyc spin on this). 

Anyway, here's the analogy. 

You can't have 40 different water internet companies competing to build network infrastructure in the same physical location. Hence, there are "natural monopolies"...you wouldn't want 40 different water sanitization companies, you would probably want ONE municipally regulated water utility (I can hear the anarcho/free-market capitalist writhing in anger). 

I'm not even say this is how it SHOULD be...I'm simply OBSERVING that this is often what HAPPENS due to the CONSTRAINTS in reality. 

To keep this incredible simple, "Western" society become the "natural monopoly" of the "modern" world...

We are all participating in political existence under the paradigm of "nation-states" - as if that is the end-all-be-all arrangement. 

We have all unknowingly inherited deep, often implicit, metaphysical assumptions about the nature of reality. 

For example, even if Hitler is allegedly "anti-Jewish" (a gross misunderstanding, but for the sake of argument) - he is still running the post-Abrahamic spiritual operating system. (For the monograph). 

So imagine you are a black kid in America. 
Your path to a successful future is to be a well-adjusted of the present order...adhering to its rules, assimilated to its values, etc

But think about it - your life must be governed by a particular paradigm of reality that "your people" had little to do with building. Whatever arbitrary "tribe" you belong to was probably not a core piece of America's self-determination as a "nation" ...

Your well-being more or less FORCES you to be a PARTICIPANT in a system that was - at least at some point - compatible with enslaving you. 

And here's the thing - it's not even that "White people's" are inherently bad or detestable...
But to conflate the COHERENCY of ANY culture's values with perfection is where the problems arise. 

Even if VAST accommodations are made to help "rectify" centuries are abuses - look at the shape...

You're still fundamentally asking an alien to assimilate and participate in YOUR paradigm of order. 

WHY should little J'Qareeus be grateful that you're offering him a pathway to the Ivy League if he sits still and applies himself inside of YOUR schools? 

Black people, for example, are being held hostage in a hostile environment where even efforts to include them actually REINFORCE the validity of the underlying assumptions that at one point might have been used to justify enslaving them...

But here is the thing! 
White people are NOT somehow inherently more evil EVEN IF the system that - essentially - the entire world-order is forced to endure IS genuinely cruel. 

And despite the ridiculous of inheriting the moral sins of the past, it's actually not THAT ridiculous...because people's souls are incubators and carriers of those values - and that gets perpetuated into the future. 

Anyway, at a deeper level - there are problems with pluralism in general. 

Imagine a Muslim who believes that homosexuality is literally against God. 
Why should they ignore GOD for the sake of "tolerance"?! 

...Why should a vegan "tolerate" the senseless slaughter of animals and subordinate their highest value in order to enshroud the value of "tolerance" that cucks them? 

Humanity has no homonoia - no like-mindedness to bring people together. 

I see it, everyone fragmenting into tribes. 

I'm exhausted by it all, but I have no time for it at the present moment. 

Jews, racism, colonizers, slavery, men, women, liberals, conservatives, socialists, Muslims, Catholics, immigrants, ICE, Indians. 

I understand why everyone is angry - I can feel it and understand everyone - on all sides. 

I am not neutral.
But I no longer operate in a frame where any of those are viable sources of order. 

I get that people are enjoying their enchanted return to ethnic identities, Islam, ideology...I appreciate that white people are finally waking up and realizing their are committing cultural suicide. And I understand why people feel like white people deserve it. 

I really do...I get all of it...
I went through my Malcolm X phase 22 years ago.
I was studying Islam 19 years ago.
My Xbox live gamertag in 2004 was "Barack Obama" - spelled correctly.
I was consuming MGTOW stuff 15 years before Andrew Tate.
I took Women and Gender studies in college nearly two decades ago.
My older sister was a vegan 30 years ago.
My mom taught me not to stand for the national anthem when I was in elementary school.
I studied the Founding Fathers.
I know the West through and through - for God's sake, I taught myself ancient Greek pre covid. 
I grew up in a neighborhood where my one row of apartments included

1. a family of 7 Nigerians
2. me
3. an older Egyptian couple
4. a family from Venezeula
5. a black/hispanic family
6. a redneck family
7. an Afghan family

I was raised around all of it - not in some urban environment like NYC with its fake "diversity" where each "community" can stick to its own. Two of my best friends were a kid from Yugoslavia...and a Muslim prince from Saudi Arabia who fell in love with Sheetz hotdogs...and we all lived in the same row of townhouses. 

I went to my first ever concert (50 cent) with a chigger fresh off the boat from South Korea, and we'd walk through the woods to our Jewish friend's house to play music in a band. And I've been to emo concerts with burly black football players and pumpkin spice white girls - staying at my Kurdish/Bengali mixed friend's house while messaging my Kurdish love interest whose family fled to Sweden as refugees. 

My neighborhood had "pinecone" wars between the South Koreans and Saudis - there were that many of them...and I can't tell you how many homes in or desi-adjacent social events I've been to where I ate something without having a single clue what it was. 

Me and my white Army Ranger buddy (RIP) who saw endless combat in Afghanistan would go fishing...while I was messaging a girl who was half-Afghan/half-Mexican about my Ghanaian girlfriend who moved from a village in Ghana to NYC - and I'd walk with her, barefoot (she insisted), connecting over the Bible while emailing the Jordanian Muslimah I was still in love with..

I had cornrows, an afro...I played in a jam band with Tool-inspired psychedelics, and I'd watch dogs for two NFL-bound black dudes while making comedy videos with a gay theater kid who was white and chubby. In college, I slept with a durag, and my girlfriend was a half-Mexican girl who was the first in her family to go to college. 

I schemed with a Taiwanese kid, an Indian kid, a Jewish kid, and a white kid to do something harmless (but illegal) to a fellow black-and-white mixed kid.  

In college I was obsessed with a Lebanese girl, in love with a Jordanian, dating the half-mexican/white girl, talking to two black mixed YouTubers😉, going on dates with a Moroccan exchange student, getting kissed on the neck by a girl from the deep south (I 100% didn't take the hint), and messaging my "friend" from Pakistan. 

I was in a band with a Peruvian bass player.

I was captain of the drumline, captain of the lacrosse team, a peer educator...I was a nerd, an athlete, an emo kid, the class clown - I went streaking with my drumline buddies in one part of the summer...church camp the next...and one of my most beloved friends was a staunch atheist...and I've been in a mosque while a guy made lewd comments about a girl's butt. 

I played drums for my church, and I was on a first-name basis with TWO imams - I ran into one of their wives yesterday...I was friends with his wife in college...I met her in my first ever econ class with a professor with a tattoo from Atlas Shrugged  (whom I loved) - while my atheist friend and I discussed the communist manifesto.

My father was a famous Muslim politician in Africa.
My grandma was the Matriarch of my family and built a thriving business in a male-dominated space. 

I grew up in government assisted housing, but I always got the latest console for Christmas. 
I know what it's like to be on food stamps...
and I know what it's like to be rich enough you feel guilty....and lonely enough to cry out of jealousy over the poor African kids my mom would sponsor because at least they looked like they belonged...

Everything I was, I was always in-between. 
Oh, and I have a TWIN SISTER...

I've been on Uber for 10+ years - I have a perfect 5-star rating - because everyone is comfortable around me...everyone thinks I'm one of them...

My white-girl friend sent me an IG real a few years ago. 
It said - if you had to send one of your friends on a completely blind "date" where they would know absolutely nothing about the other person, but they had to get along with that person - who would you send? 

Me, of course

Because I get it....I really do.

But don't worry...
I'm about to make all of your differences irrelevant.

text:
The Saleh–Ogenga "Consociational Democracy Agreement," Part 4: Dead on Arrival

I will comment on the operational framework, the structures, chambers and diagrams, in a later post. Before we discuss how to operationalise an agreement, we must ask whether it can stand at all. I welcome this paper as the beginning of a conversation. Ugandans have long demanded a reckoning with exclusion, and it matters that a document from the heart of the regime now names it. But beginning a conversation is not the same as settling it, and in its current form the Agreement is dead on arrival. Here is why.

1. Its motivation. The paper calls for politics organised "around grand coalitions or cooperation, rather than simple majority." It says power sharing works only once elites "accept that unilateral victory is impossible." That is a remarkable admission from a party that has claimed majorities for forty years. It is not a sudden awakening of conscience about exclusive rule. It reads like a regime that no longer trusts the ballot to carry it, looking for a new formula for continuity. As I showed in Part 3, every Ugandan regime turns to "broad-based" arrangements when it is in trouble.
2. Its authors, and what that does to trust. The paper's first test for success is that the Agreement "must be a written, public document — not a backroom arrangement," and it warns that opaque elite deals "eroded public trust." By its own standard it has already failed. It was conceived and written by two men, one of them the President's brother and a central figure in the very system of patronage the paper refuses to name. It then asks the rest of us to co-sign, gazette and fund it before anyone else has spoken. A reconciliation process cannot have its terms written in advance by one side.
3. Without trust, there is no reconciliation.The paper says credible elections and independent institutions are "vital to generate trust and genuine legitimacy rather than managed acquiescence." Yet it puts doubts about the Electoral Commission in the mouths of "some political parties and civil society," who "claimed" a crisis of credibility. It wants to remove only the "negative" involvement of security forces, as if there were a positive one. It treats the EC's own figures as gospel. Meanwhile, party presidents are in jail or in exile, Dr. Besigye is denied bail, and the High Court has had to order the State to account for Sam Mugumya after 440 days. Asking for consensus under those conditions produces exactly the "managed acquiescence" the paper warns against. Reconciliation needs trust, and trust has to be earned first.
4. It refuses to look in the mirror. The paper credits the NRM with "tremendous socio-economic and political achievements" against exclusion and sectarianism, and "more sustained progress than any predecessor." It is silent on what earlier governments achieved and on what Structural Adjustment cost ordinary Ugandans. It says nothing about abductions, torture, or the concentration of power in the army.  If the NRM had done such a tremendous job, why do we need this Agreement? You cannot cure a disease if you refuse to say who caused it.
The paper describes how pre-colonial rulers drew legitimacy from founders elevated "through myths, fictions, invented histories and strategic memories" to "the status of demi gods." Read alongside the paper's praise of the President's "unwavering commitment," that passage describes what this document itself is doing: placing the 1986 liberators above everyone else to secure continuity. It is not looking for partners. It is looking for followers.
5. It names exclusion but offers no remedy for it. The paper's subject is political and economic exclusion and the concentration of power in a small group. Apart from more money for education, it offers no mechanism to fix that. It says nothing about power sharing in the security services, nothing about rebalancing recruitment, promotion and retirement, and nothing about an audit of who holds which posts. Without those, "consociation" just means admitting a few new people into the existing order.
6. We have been here before. The paper itself recalls the Uganda National Dialogue, launched on 1 November 2019 after two years of consultations with about 3,000 citizens and the Inter-Religious Council, the Elders Forum, IPOD, CCEDU, the Women Situation Room and others. It stalled. Before that came the Odoki Commission's grassroots consultations, the Constituent Assembly and the 1995 Constitution, whose term limits and age limit were later removed. Why didn't those deliver, and what makes this attempt different? The paper doesn't say.
7. Consociation needs equals. Lijphart's models, the Netherlands, Belgium, Austria and Switzerland, were bargains among free elites who could walk away from the table. Closer to home, the power-sharing deals that followed disputed elections, Kenya in 2008 and Zimbabwe in 2009, show the risk. In Zimbabwe, the unity government gave the incumbent time to regroup, and ZANU-PF returned to full control in 2013. When one party holds the army, the purse and the prisons, power sharing becomes a way for the incumbent to survive.

What must come first. This Agreement must be taken apart and rebuilt before we talk about operationalising it: 
• Release political prisoners and stop the abductions. 
• Commission an independent, public audit of who holds power in the army, security, civil service, MDAs, parastatals and oil. (Plus other public spaces) 
• Hand the process to a convenor not chosen by the State, with the opposition, civil society, religious leaders, the diaspora and victims at the table as co-authors rather than co-signatories. 
• Honour the 1995 Constitution as the floor, not the ceiling.

Then we can talk. Until then, this is a monologue dressed up as dialogue.

text:
Why Did Hermione Granger Get an 'E' in Defense Against the Dark Arts?

Hermione Granger’s O.W.L.s have one famous blemish: an 'E' in Defense Against the Dark Arts.

The culprit wasn't Dolores Umbridge's magic ban. It was a simple truth: you cannot memorize a Boggart.

While Hermione excels at magic that requires logic, precise wand movements, and rote memorization, Defense Against the Dark Arts demands instinct, improvisation, and the nerve to react to unpredictable fear.

In her third year, Hermione completely failed her practical Boggart exam when it turned into Professor McGonagall telling her she had failed all her subjects.

Harry Potter, by contrast, relies on survival instincts and combat reflexes honed by actual encounters with dark magic, giving him a natural edge in high-pressure practical defense.

Harry's Extraordinary O.W.L. Performance

Harry’s extraordinary performance during the O.W.L.s also skewed the expected standard.

During the practical portion, Professor Tofty offered Harry a bonus point to produce a Patronus.

Summoning a fully corporeal Patronus at age fifteen was practically unheard of.

Harry’s mastery of combat magic firmly placed him at the 'Outstanding' tier, making Hermione's 'E' a realistic reflection of her slightly less instinctual combat abilities.

Dolores Umbridge's Restrictions

The political environment surrounding their fifth year made passing the exam at all a minor miracle, entirely due to Dolores Umbridge.

Installed by a paranoid Ministry of Magic to prevent Albus Dumbledore from training a student militia, Umbridge stripped the curriculum down to reading Wilbert Slinkhard’s Defensive Magical Theory.

Students were forbidden from even drawing their wands in class.

Umbridge enforced her regime by blanketing the school walls with Educational Decrees, eventually banning all student organizations.

Recognizing they would fail their practical exams and remain entirely defenseless against Voldemort, Hermione convinced Harry to form the secret defensive group known as Dumbledore's Army (D.A.).

The Irony of Dumbledore's Army

By suppressing practical education, Umbridge achieved the exact opposite of her goal.

She inadvertently forced the students underground, where they received elite, hands-on combat instruction from Harry.

When the Ministry's independent examiners arrived at the end of the year, they tested the students on actual spellcasting Boggarts, shielding charms, and levitation not Umbridge's theoretical textbook.

The D.A. members ultimately thrived on their exams precisely because they had to circumvent their own professor to learn the material.
