text:
“For you is your religion, and for me is my religion.” [Al-Kafirun 109:6]

The distinction between permissible relations and religious participation is established in the revealed texts. Your appeal to historical governance does not erase it.

You then argue that lighting candles during Diwali is outright disbelief if performed as religious participation but insignificant if performed as a gesture of political respect.

Where is your evidence that political intention automatically changes the ruling upon an outward religious act?

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

“Actions are only by intentions, and every person shall have only what he intended.”

Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim

This hadith does not establish that good intentions automatically render prohibited actions permissible. The nature of the action must also be considered.

If a Muslim politician offered incense before a Hindu deity but claimed he intended only political respect, would that make the offering permissible? If he participated in the Christian Eucharist while claiming to represent Christian constituents, would that cease to be religious participation? If he joined a Zoroastrian devotional ceremony involving sacred fire, would political courtesy remove its religious character?

What if he made a devotional offering at a Buddhist shrine, participated in an invocation to a Hindu deity or joined Christian Christmas worship for electoral purposes?

Would you dismiss objections to all these practices as political ignorance and pearl-clutching?

If your answer is no, then you concede that political representation has religious boundaries. If your answer is yes, produce your evidence from the Quran, authentic Sunnah and from ah Ilm.

A Muslim may represent Christians without receiving Communion, Hindus without performing puja, Buddhists without making devotional offerings and Zoroastrians without participating in their religious rites.

Political representation is not religious participation, and political courtesy does not independently make prohibited worship permissible.

Your comparison between lighting ceremonial candles in a Hindu temple and a non Muslim removing his shoes before entering a mosque is an astonishingly defective analogy.

Removing shoes is ordinarily an act of etiquette. Making a religious offering or performing a devotional ceremony is an entirely different legal category.

The mere fact that both actions occur within religious buildings does not make them equivalent.

The relevant question is whether the candle lighting constituted an actual religious rite, participation in a distinctive religious celebration or an ordinary non devotional gesture. Calling it political does not answer that question.

There is also evidence from the Sunnah concerning religious practices inherited from non-Muslim communities.

Anas ibn Malik رضي الله عنه narrated that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ arrived in Madinah, its people had two days on which they celebrated. He asked about them, and they explained that these were days of celebration from the pre-Islamic period.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

“Allah has substituted for you something better than them: the Day of al-Adha and the Day of al-Fitr.”

Sunan Abi Dawud

The Prophet ﷺ distinguished the religious celebrations of Islam from those inherited from Jahiliyyah. He did not preserve them merely because they were established community customs.

Abu Waqid al-Laythi رضي الله عنه narrated that some people who had recently embraced Islam asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to appoint for them a Dhat Anwat, resembling the sacred tree used by the polytheists.

The Prophet ﷺ strongly condemned their request and compared it to the statement of the Children of Israel:

اجعل لنا إلها كما لهم آلهة

“Make for us a god just as they have gods.” [Al-Araf 7:138]

Jami al-Tirmidhi

text:
November 9

                Praise with Your Hands

“Lift up your hands in the sanctuary, And bless the LORD.” —Psalm 134:2 (NKJV)

Psalm 134 is the last of the fifteen Songs of Ascents, the collection of psalms associated with pilgrims going up to Jerusalem. This final song turns to “all you servants of the LORD, who by night stand in the house of the LORD.” These were likely Levites serving through the night, keeping watch and carrying out their duties while most of the city slept.

The psalm calls them to turn those hidden hours into worship: “Lift up your hands in the sanctuary, and bless the LORD.” Then the final verse answers that worship with a blessing: “The LORD who made heaven and earth bless you from Zion.”

The key word is the Hebrew nasa (naw-SAW), translated “lift up.” It means to lift, carry, or bear. The same verb appears in the priestly blessing: “The LORD lift up His countenance upon you, and give you peace” (Numbers 6:26).

That gives us a beautiful picture. God’s people lift their hands toward Him in worship, and God lifts His face toward His people in blessing.

Think of a nurse on night duty in a district hospital. The ward is quiet, most patients are asleep, and there is no audience to applaud the work being done. She checks a drip, turns a patient, responds to a call bell, and keeps watch through the small hours.

Psalm 134 speaks into that kind of hidden service.

The temple servants stood at their posts through the night, and the psalm invited them to lift their hands and bless the Lord right there. Their work was not separate from worship. The hidden place became a place of praise.

Raised hands are a simple biblical expression of worship. Scripture also shows people bowing, kneeling, standing, and falling before God. The posture itself is not the point. The body is simply joining the heart in turning toward Him.

There are times when lifting your hands says what words struggle to express.

It can say, “Lord, I surrender.”
It can say, “I need You.”
It can say, “I honour You.”

It can also say, “These hands are empty, but they are Yours.”

So when you serve in places few people notice, remember that God sees you. Your work may happen on a night shift, in a quiet office, in your home, or in responsibilities that receive very little recognition.

Lift your hands to Him there.
Offer the hidden work to Him.
Let your service become worship.

And receive the words that close the psalm: “The LORD who made heaven and earth bless you from Zion.”

The work may be hidden from people, but it is never hidden from God.

Confession:
In the hidden hours I lift my hands to the Lord and bless Him. I offer Him the work I do when no one is watching. My hands belong to Him, and my service becomes worship. The Lord sees me, lifts His countenance upon me, and gives me peace.

text:
What’s Actually at Risk?

The risk is 2029. 
Projects already under construction cover only about 20% of the capacity expected to come online in 2029. 
The other 80% still needs a permit, and that’s exactly where the new rules bite. 
So, the next question is: what would the new rules mean for the capacity not yet under construction? 
I think the best way to understand it is to see what electoral candidates are demanding from datacenters. 
Let’s look at Gina Hinojosa — Texas’s Governor-elect. 
Texas has the second-largest share of compute capacity, and legislation there will act as a precedent for other states to follow. 
Gina wants legislation passed to ‘protect the communities’ that host the datacenters. 
(Virginia’s Loudoun County budget now has $1 Bn+ in datacenter tax revenue funding public infrastructure… If that’s what being harmed looks like, most counties would sign up tomorrow.) 
This legislation would require that data centers: 
(1) pay taxes 
» Yes, of course large tech companies should pay taxes. And, many already contribute to their communities where there is effective local governance. 
(2) pledge not to raise residents’ electricity rates 
» that means more behind-the-grid solutions, which is what datacenters are already doing with nuclear energy and nat gas providers. 
(3) protect residents’ access to water 
» Texas datacenters touch 0.46% of water. This is fearmongering, not a real issue. And voters don’t rank datacenters as a top issue. 
(4) use union labor during construction. 
» Mark Zuckerberg is spending over $115M on training blue-collar workers… Big Tech companies will spend on union labor. 
What’s the bottom line? 
(1) All of the demands on datacenters will be fulfilled. (Don’t forget hyperscalers are major contributors to the Democrat Party, and Anthropic has a lot of ex-Biden era staffers. This is 80% political theater, and 20% substance.) 
(2) 2026 & 2027 datacenter build is intact, per Texas’s Governor-elect. So, the debate is around 2028. And, there’s plenty of time for policymakers to resolve that. 
The Returns Are Too Good to Walk Away From
The hyperscalers are earning returns north of 30% on their invested capital. Their cost of capital is a fraction of that. 
That creates a huge cushion. 
These projects still make sense if they cost two or three times as much to build.  
Double the cost, and a 30% return is still about 15%. 
Look at the commitments. 
Anthropic’s IPO filing shows nearly $900 billion of compute and infrastructure commitments running out to 2045, some on 20-year take-or-pay contracts. 
And, the industry is already adapting. 
OpenAI is already working with communities to mitigate the negatives around datacenter construction. 
Sarah Friar (CFO, OpenAI) listed what OpenAI offers host communities: a promise never to raise local electricity bills, recycled water, a 300-foot berm in Georgia to block the noise, and free school lunches and a park. 
(Imagine getting a politician to honor their commitments!) 
Management finds a way. 
Nvidia has approached Apollo about converting more than 130 old telecom buildings into AI data centers. 
Existing infra means existing power and fewer fights.

TEXAS INSTRUMENTS $TXN HAS ITS BEST DAY SINCE JUNE:

Texas Instruments (TXN) at $295.73, +$18.37 / +6.62% on Monday.

Texas Instruments still passes the Quality Len5, and is on none of the other Len5es we weigh, after its biggest one-day gain since June 18. The gain, about $17B of market value, came with other makers of analog chips, the parts that turn sound, heat and pressure into data, and no outlet tied it to any news from Texas Instruments that day. The shares have won back about half of Thursday's fall. Texas Instruments's own financial news on Monday was $2B of new notes, a kind of bond. They are its first borrowing to buy Silicon Labs (SLAB) at $221.80, +$0.30 / +0.14% on Monday. Texas Instruments has a loan of up to $5B lined up for the same purchase, and borrowing most of it would take its debt past the Quality Len5's limit as its books stood on September 30.

The Quality Len5 wants a profit and debt no larger than the owners' equity, the money shareholders have in the business, and Texas Instruments's September 30 books, with Monday's notes added, still show both:
- Profit in the September quarter: $2.43B.
- Debt: about $15.5B, from $13.56B.
- Owners' equity: $19.19B.
What would knock it off the Quality Len5: more than about $3.6B of new borrowing, with equity where it stood on September 30. Momentum wants a stock near its high, and Monday's close is 11.0% under June 22's closing high of $332.28; closes back toward it would put Texas Instruments on the Momentum Len5.

24/7 Wall St. called Monday's gains a sector-wide analog chip rally and wrote that the available facts do not show what drove it. CNBC tied last week's selling to investors rethinking data-center building after Democrats won control of Congress.
- VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) at $487.41, +$23.45 / +5.05% on Monday.
- Thursday, the day of our post: -$33.34 / -10.70%, to $278.15.
- Friday and Monday together, since our post: +$17.58 / +6.3%.
Our read: buyers came back to chipmakers as a group on Monday, the way sellers left them as a group on Thursday.

We wrote on Thursday that Monday's $2B was the first fact that could cost Texas Instruments its Quality Len5 standing. The notes were issued on Monday, in four groups that come due from 2028 to 2036, and Texas Instruments still passes. The money goes toward the roughly $7.5B price of Silicon Labs. Texas Instruments agreed in February to buy the Austin maker of wireless chips for $231 a share in cash. If the purchase is called off or runs past its deadline, Texas Instruments must buy the notes back at 101 cents on the dollar. Silicon Labs is on none of the Len5es we weigh; it lost money in its last fiscal year, and the cash offer sets its price, with Monday's close 4.0% under it.

Texas Instruments arranged the loan of up to $5B in June for the Silicon Labs price and had borrowed none of it by September 30, when it held $8.1B of cash and short-term investments. Monday's $2B leaves its debt smaller than its owners' equity. Year-end books arrive with a report tentatively set for January 26. Texas Instruments expects to close the purchase, and pay for it, in the first half of 2027, once foreign regulators approve it.

Not investment advice.

There's always uncertainty & lies in what both sides say in war. Truth is usually somewhere else but the general rule of thumb is that winners don't need to lie as much. Here's what we do know about the Gaza war so far:-

*Total deaths are just over 70,000 so far out of a Gazan population estimated at around 2.2 million & still growing.

*The ratio of civilians to combatants killed is exceptionally low. 1.39:1 on Hamas figures (ie:-claimed) & <2:1 & nearing 1:1 for some actions as claimed by Israel.

*Hamas claimed to have only killed 4,000 of their own civilians themselves. This is despite refusing offers of demilitarised safe areas for their civilians early in the conflict, actively trying to prevent civilians from escaping from areas about to become attacked & having a history of killing & maiming Gazan civilians as a means of maintaining their control. Add to that misfiring rockets etc.

*Hamas uses Gazan civilians, the majority of whom were their supporters as human shields, tries to get as many of them killed as possible to help their war with Israel & hides amongst them & in tunnels under their most densely packed neighbourhoods.

*Hamas spent billions on concrete bunkers & tunnel complexes for themselves & never built one bomb shelter for their Gazan civilians. When asked a notable Hamas leader is quoted as saying 'that is the UN's job'.

*Gaza MoH have published a list of names of the dead which can & has been matched with published ID numbers. Numerous anomalies became apparent. Men listed as women. Adults listed as children. Known Hamas & IJ listed as civilian war deaths, people who died of old age & with cancer in hospital in Israel listed as having been killed in the war etc.

Much more than this will be hard to confirm until the war is over & perhaps better data becomes available. Maybe not even then. What is transparently obvious is that there's been no genocide. No attempt. No intent & in fact there's been a notable absence of high rates of civilian casualties typical of wars up until now.

injective-protocol:native  — INJECTIVE
⠀
An $804 MILLION cryptocurrency.
⠀
A blockchain built specifically for decentralized finance.
⠀
Approximately $222 MILLION in weekly perpetual trading volume.
⠀
And a token with a built-in buyback-and-burn mechanism.
⠀
But here's the contradiction.
⠀
Injective has one of crypto's more interesting token-economic designs.
⠀
Its ecosystem supports trading, derivatives, staking, and financial applications.
⠀
Yet its DeFi TVL is only around $18.6 million.
⠀
And despite its reputation as a deflationary asset, new INJ continues to be issued.
⠀
Even more importantly, major price aggregators report 100 million tokens, while a recent SEC filing identifies approximately 122.9 million in total supply.
⠀
Is injective-protocol:native an overlooked financial infrastructure investment?
⠀
Or is the market correctly discounting weak adoption and uncertain net supply dynamics?
⠀
Let's examine the numbers.
⠀
01 | WHAT IS INJECTIVE?
⠀
Injective is a Layer 1 blockchain designed for financial applications.
⠀
Its infrastructure supports:
⠀
• Decentralized spot trading
• Perpetual derivatives
• On-chain order books
• Real-world asset applications
• Staking and governance
• Cross-chain connectivity
• Token buybacks and burns
⠀
Its objective is to provide infrastructure for programmable financial markets.
⠀
But strong infrastructure does not automatically guarantee strong token demand.
⠀
02 | THE NUMBERS THAT MATTER
⠀
November 10, 2026 snapshot:
⠀
INJ Price: ~$8.04
⠀
Reported Market Cap: ~$804M
⠀
Reported FDV: ~$804M
⠀
Aggregator Circulating Supply: ~100M INJ
⠀
Reported Maximum Supply: 100M INJ
⠀
DeFi TVL: ~$18.6M
⠀
Stablecoin Market Cap: ~$16.1M
⠀
24H DEX Volume: ~$858K
⠀
24H Perpetual Volume: ~$24.7M
⠀
7D Perpetual Volume: ~$222M
⠀
All-Time High: ~$52.75
⠀
Decline From ATH: ~84.8%
⠀
But there is a major supply-data discrepancy.
⠀
A November 2026 SEC filing describes approximately 122.9 million INJ in total supply as of September 15.
⠀
That means the commonly reported 100 million maximum supply should not be treated as a verified hard cap.
⠀
03 | THE FINANCIAL INFRASTRUCTURE OPPORTUNITY
⠀
Injective targets one of crypto's largest economic sectors.
⠀
On-chain financial markets.
⠀
Potential applications include:
⠀
• Perpetual futures
• Spot exchanges
• Tokenized financial assets
• Structured products
• Automated trading
• Institutional DeFi
⠀
The opportunity is significant.
⠀
But Injective competes against established trading infrastructure and other specialized blockchains.
⠀
The critical metric is not how many financial products can theoretically be built.
⠀
It's how many users consistently trade and pay for those products.
⠀
04 | THE TOKEN BURN MECHANISM
⠀
INJ has a mechanism that connects ecosystem activity to token supply.
⠀
Historically, Injective used weekly burn auctions.
⠀
A portion of application fees was accumulated and auctioned in exchange for INJ.
⠀
The INJ received was permanently burned.
⠀
In October 2025, this system transitioned to the Community BuyBack mechanism.
⠀
Participants commit INJ in exchange for a proportional share of eligible ecosystem revenue assets.
⠀
The committed INJ is burned.
⠀
This creates a direct relationship between participating ecosystem revenue and token destruction.
⠀
But the size of that benefit depends on actual revenue and participation.
⠀
A burn mechanism is only as economically significant as the amount of supply it removes.
⠀
05 | THE SUPPLY CONTRADICTION
⠀
This is the most important part of the INJ investment thesis.
⠀
INJ does not have a permanently fixed total supply.
⠀
New tokens are issued through staking rewards.
⠀
Tokens are also removed through buyback-and-burn mechanisms.
⠀
According to a recent SEC filing:
⠀
September 15, 2026 Total Supply:
⠀
Approximately 122.9M INJ.
⠀
INJ Bonded to Validators:
⠀
Approximately 58M.
⠀
Bonded Share:
⠀
Approximately 47.2%.
⠀
The filing also identifies an annual issuance-rate range of 2.2% to 4.4% at that time.
⠀
The actual rate depends on staking participation and governance parameters.
⠀
Therefore, investors must distinguish:
⠀
Gross issuance.
⠀
Tokens burned.
⠀
Net supply change.
⠀
And circulating supply.
⠀
INJ can burn tokens while total supply still increases.
⠀
06 | THE 2026 SUPPLY SQUEEZE
⠀
In January 2026, Injective governance approved the INJ Supply Squeeze proposal.
⠀
The initiative was designed to tighten issuance parameters and strengthen the network's deflationary mechanics.
⠀
But here's the distinction.
⠀
A policy intended to accelerate supply reduction is not proof that total supply is already declining.
⠀
The actual outcome depends on:
⠀
• New token issuance
• Staking participation
• Ecosystem revenue
• Buyback participation
• Tokens permanently burned
⠀
The strongest evidence is a sustained reduction in net supply.
⠀

text:
GPU-related businesses are arising hard.

The simplest model is to supply the million-dollar cost GPU cluster on-chain so that operators can hire them, not to own the whole hardware infra.

I'm choosing these 3 frontiers that work in this field by in different approaches.

+ @USDai_Official: making loans secured by GPUs
+ @falconfinance: a collateral and stablecoin adding one GPU instrument, a tokenized forward, as a pilot
+ @gaib_ai: packaging GPU and robotics financing deals into a yield-bearing token

Let's see how they differ:

1. Background

+ USDai: $17.4M fund raised in different rounds, TGE happened in Apr 21, 2026; with credit hub now running on Arbitrum.

+ Falcon: did not start with GPU, its GPU financing is the first product in a regulated tokenization pipeline it opened in El Salvador on Aug 18, 2026.

+ GAIB: $15M raised in funding, GAIB is an economic layer for AI infra, not only GPUs; mainnet launched in Oct 31, 2025.

2. How each approaches GPUs

+ USDai: lending against the hardware

Borrowers are AI infrastructure operators and loans are non-recourse to the GPUs and their contracted cash flows, with recourse to the borrower only for fraud.

Supported hardwares: NVIDIA B300, B200, GB300, RTX 6000 and RTX 5090; with loan-to-value of about 70–80%.

The largest loan so far is $98.1 million to Duos Edge AI for 2,304 NVIDIA B300 GPUs.

+ Falcon: financing the wait for delivery

Its GPU forward funds the months gap between paying for high-end GPUs and installing them.

NEAR AI is the anchor buyer of the compute the GPUs will produce, vGPU supplies, installs and services the equipment. The intention is for the instrument to trade on open venues such as Uniswap and, once it has enough depth, serve as collateral to mint USDf.

+ GAIB: packaging deals into a vault

GAIB sources and underwrites financing deals with GPU operators and cloud providers, then funnels them into sAID.

Example: a reported $30M GPU financing for Thailand's SiamAI and an H200-based deployment on Aethir's network.

Collaterals have an active resale market, with recourse through liquidation or continued hosting.

3. Operational metrics

+ USDai: $157.82M in TVL (contributed as $USDai), base apy offered by USDai via sUSDai holding is around 6.5%.

+ Falcon: $1.66B in TVL (contributed as $USDf), GPU forward size not disclosed.

+ GAIB: around $15m of TVL (contributed as sAID), 10.44% base apy on Ethereum

Final takes:

+ USDai is the clearest GPU-credit product, with the biggest loan book, but about half of its capital sits in a cash-like reserve.

+ Falcon is a stablecoin platform trying a GPU pilot, and its supply matters more to its health than its GPU deal.

+ GAIB has the longest focus on GPU financing and a steady vault yield, but its scale has fallen well below its early campaign peak.

Which one is your fav?

He also backed the resumption of the South Caucasus regional 3+3 platform, which Georgia has so far refused to join, citing Russia’s occupation of its territories. text:
Here is the rebuttal to your Part One. Whoever wrote it leaves a lot of things out and is very disingenuous. 

Jefferson did not remain silent on the charges. In a letter of July 1, 1805, to Secretary of the Navy Robert Smith, he directly addressed the “antient slanders” then circulating. He wrote that he pleaded guilty to only one of the accusations against him: “that when young and single I offered love to a handsome lady” (the Walker affair). He called this “the only one founded in truth among all their allegations against me.” The letter referenced an enclosed, more detailed response to Attorney General Levi Lincoln that has not survived, but the cover letter to Smith does exist and shows Jefferson privately denying the bulk of the charges while admitting the one he regarded as accurate. He was never a man who sought public confrontations or duels; had he been, he would have faced Hamilton far earlier over far more serious public disagreements. Callender, the source of the most scurrilous attacks, was a ruined and discredited figure by 1803, when he died. Jefferson had little to gain by further engagement with a man already widely regarded as untrustworthy.

The claim that John Wayles was Sally Hemings’s father rests almost entirely on later oral testimony from Isaac Jefferson and Madison Hemings. Isaac Jefferson was not a Wayles family slave; he was born around 1775, roughly two years after Wayles’s death in May 1773, so he could only have reported family lore rather than direct knowledge. Madison Hemings’s 1873 account is likewise family tradition recorded long after the events. 

Contemporary or near-contemporary references, such as the 1805 piece signed by T. Turner of Wheatland, do not establish personal knowledge of events that allegedly occurred before the writer’s birth; Turner was a child at the relevant time. Wayles was ill in the final years of his life and traveled little. Sally Hemings was born around 1773—sources place her birth in that year, and she was an infant when the Hemings family was inherited by Martha Jefferson after Wayles’s death. The possibility that she was born after Wayles’s death cannot be ruled out on the surviving evidence, and the entire case for his paternity depends on accounts generated decades later. Such testimony would not meet the standards of a court of law.

It is true that household slaves lived in close proximity to Jefferson and that the boundary between master and household servant was often spatial. Yet no contemporaneous eyewitness reported seeing anything more than ordinary household interaction between Jefferson and his slaves. The one overseer who left a detailed account, Edmund Bacon, stated the opposite: he reported seeing another man leaving Sally Hemings’s room on multiple mornings and specifically denied that Harriet Hemings was Jefferson’s daughter. (Bacon’s employment dates and the reliability of later transcriptions of his remarks have been debated, but his is the only direct overseer testimony on the point.)

text:
Van Gogh's paintings only sold after his sister-in-law published his letters. Bugzy Malone takes it as a reason to do your best work for people not yet born.

Takeaways from Bugzy Malone (@TheBugzyMalone) on Modern Wisdom (@ChrisWillx) 👇

1. Making it and maintaining it are different games, and almost nobody talks about the second
Bugzy says we are advertised to as kids to chase the cars and clothes of people who have made it. Nobody warns you about maintenance, so many people shoot up, plateau and fall off. Chris adds that advice is aimed at the climb because most people are still climbing. Bugzy’s album is about this underdocumented phase after you have told your story and spent the money: “What next? That’s maintain it.”

2. What you are praised for in public you often pay for in private
Chris tells of a Navy SEAL whose “I don’t quit” identity kept him in a toxic marriage for 15 years. A strength can become a constraint. Bugzy agrees that nobody wants to talk about the cost of building a new self. Moving from poverty and dysfunction to an affluent, functional place means parts of you have to die. Ask what your own achievements have cost.

3. Adversity is a sparring partner: it gives you only what you can handle, and belief has to become your own
Bugzy compares hard childhood experiences to a boxing coach putting you in the ring with someone better. His coach Brian Hughes had him sparring with an older boxer who was beating him. Brian told him to throw the uppercut they had practised, and it landed. He learned to see in himself what his coach saw, and he came to believe faith is a journey you walk alone. He now reads early challenges as preparation, not victimhood.

4. Remove every crutch: self-reliance beats collecting friends who believe in you more than you do
Chris suggests finding friends who believe in you more than you do. Bugzy disagrees. He thinks the harder and better path is stripping away every crutch, because people may say they believe in you and then doubt you privately. Only once you are self-reliant do you have something to offer friends. Bugzy says the same about manufacturing enemies for motivation: it is farmed energy, a crutch, and the real fuel is love.

5. People discredit those who rise because progress exposes their own lack of it
Bugzy says people stuck in a victim mindset discredit someone who has moved on, because they cannot explain how he did it. Chris says progress by others closes the gap by making it look like luck, cheating or nepotism. Bugzy’s answer is ruthless accountability. The footballer made it because he did the extra runs while you were chilling. Admitting that gives you the chance to pick again.

6. The tunnel: success means walking through isolation and ridicule until you face your fears
Bugzy’s analogy for the path to success is a tunnel. Those who stay behind ridicule you, then you lose sight of the entrance and the exit. You step on the remains of those who failed, and the only option is to keep marching. The solitude costs you familiar people and a familiar world. He says facing your insecurities there unlocks a version of you that people can no longer pull down.

7. Fear hidden from only grows: you eventually have to come out of the house and fight it
At 11, Bugzy was stabbed in the leg with a screwdriver. He hid at home for about three years, fearful and ashamed, and reached suicidal thoughts. He only recovered by facing the boy in a fair fight on that estate, which he won. His lesson is that you can hide as long as you like, but eventually you must face what scares you. He adds that not every fight is for now, and some can wait.

8. Rap is a young man’s game, so diversify before the next phase arrives
Bugzy says rapping is about the come-up and escaping dysfunction, and lingering too long is a risk. He notes that boxers and footballers who don’t diversify gain weight, spend money on addictions and end up sad. He is moving into acting, with The Gentleman series 3, and plans a rap part two when he is a husband and father. He wants the transferable skills to apply to an adult job.

9. Early motivation like a chip on the shoulder is toxic fuel, and the real fuel is love
Chris asks what happens when the fuel of proving people wrong runs out. Bugzy admits he has tried to produce that fuel by provoking himself with rivals, which made him train and read more. He calls it a crutch that relies on something external. The real fuel, he says, is love: he remembers being a 12-year-old watching Muhammad Ali and finding inspiration. He knows a kid out there takes strength from what he does next.

10. Your psychological immune system flags toxic patterns, but maturity turns reactions into responsible decisions
Chris compares chronic inflammatory response syndrome to being triggered by echoes of a harmful childhood environment: the body reacts to a tiny dose of a familiar threat. Bugzy likens this to airbags deploying prematurely. As you mature, you weigh up a situation and set healthy boundaries. For him the right word is responsibility: you decide to walk away instead of just reacting.

11. Freedom has three layers (you money, you freedom, you family) and psychological security matters most
Chris describes three kinds of you: money, freedom, and a family that makes you feel like a superhero. Bugzy says you need all three, because without money you can’t get real freedom, and a family won’t stay if you aren’t functional. Chris argues the kingdom that matters most is emotional. Bugzy agrees that the external reflects the internal and that the journey is internal and involves solitude.

12. Do your best work for people not yet born: Van Gogh’s letters made his paintings valuable
Bugzy says Van Gogh’s paintings sold only after his sister-in-law published his letters, which let people understand his mindset. He finds a lesson in the film Eternity’s Gate, where Van Gogh feels God made him a painter “for people that haven’t yet been born”. Bugzy concludes that his influence may come after he is gone, so he should do his best work and not get lazy when people can’t see all the layers.

🚨Oregon, here are the findings of the Nov 3rd SEL pull & some initial anomalies that stuck out. 

1⃣Oregon has more registrations than adults (109%)

The voter file has 3.8 million registrations against about 3.48 million adults (18+), using PSU's 2025 estimate. 

Counting only "active" voters it's 89%, which is normal, so the excess may be the "inactive" records Judicial Watch sued over. 

Klamath & Columbia County are near 120%

Josephine County is at 119%. 

Wallowa is the one county with more "active" voters than adults, by about 224.

2⃣Non-residential addresses

1,090 Active voters list 650 NW Irving St in Portland as home. That's a homeless resource center that offers mail service. 

Another 256 list the Portland Rescue Mission

93 list JOIN's day center. 

3⃣ 19 people died but were listed as "active" voters! 

Oregon mails a ballot to every 'active' voter. 

4⃣VERY old voters.

Oregon has two active voters who are 111!

Born in 1915 or 1916 who voted in 2024 & in the May 2026 primary.

Another in Lincoln County & one in Yamhill. 

Overall, 85 records would be 110 or older, mostly classified as "inactive" 

3,342 are 100 or older.

Multiple SI also claim it's very odd especially as the 2020 Census counted only 969 Oregonians aged 100 or older. Even with steady growth, that should only be around 1,100.

3,342 is 3X way too many. 

5⃣Duplicate voters

There are 70 possible duplicate voters in the same county. 

These are pairs with the same first, middle, and last name and birth year, both "active" and both voting in 2024 (Multnomah 19, Clackamas 13, Washington 9). They could be twins or typos. 
If both records in a pair vote again on Nov 3, that's a real red flag. 

369 Polk County Active voters have a registration date of 11-11-1111. That's a placeholder date, a sign of sloppy data rather than fraud, but it means the county is not listing when they actually registered.

2,545 Active voters have out-of-state mailing addresses, mostly UO students in Lane County. 

Spikes in registrations match the deadline, the party switches are ordinary, and almost no PO boxes are used as home addresses.

The Nov 3 voting history will be available either December or January and should settle who of the above actually voted.

Meet Preston Means (he/they), President of Oriel College, Oxford MCR, University of Oxford, in the college's 700th year.

Hailing from the Great Plains of Kansas, Preston came to Oxford after an undergraduate degree in Psychology, Sociology, and Political Science at The University of Kansas (Rock Chalk!).

Preston has just finished their MSc in Politics Research at Department of Politics and International Relations, University of Oxford, where they researched how exploration of queer identity challenges assumptions around the political socialization process. Now a 1st-year DPhil student in Politics, they hope to expand on this work and explore how queer and political identities interact and shape one another.

Working closely with the Oriel MCR community, Oriel JCR, Oriel College, the Students' Union, and the Conference of Common Rooms, they have been furthering their committee's vision of an Oriel MCR that promotes respect for all, in line with the University of Oxford's commitment to the same. Preston joined other common rooms in calling an Extraordinary Conference of Common Rooms tomorrow to raise an item on speaker events. He is dedicated to shaping the Oriel MCR into an environment that celebrates the breadth of diverse experiences in its student body and reaffirms the value of every student who walks through its doors.

Oriel College, Oxford is known for its rowing prowess. As of Summer Eights 2026, the men's first boat is Head of the River and the men's second is the highest second boat on the river. Every women's crew made multiple bumps, and none were bumped down.

Fun fact: the Provost's lodgings have a cat door! It was built for the pet cat of the head of house in 2003 and completed in 2004.

Preston had a tour of the Oxford SU. Coffee's on me is the standing offer: two lattes.

Making that time for our student representatives - to learn from them, and support them better in the year ahead - is what I most want to protect.

text:
Fake job offers aren't just a scam on job hunters any more. They're being used to break into companies. Here are the warning signs.

Red flags, per Action Fraud:
→ A job you never applied for, out of the blue
→ "You've got the job" without a real interview
→ Any fee: for the application, checks, a visa or training
→ Asking for your bank details "to set up your salary" early
→ A recruiter writing from a free webmail address

For developers and tech workers, the FBI adds:
→ A "coding test" that asks you to download and run someone else's code
→ Pressure to install unusual software for a simple video call

What to do: check the company yourself, contact it only via its official site, and never run a test file on a work laptop.

Why it matters: Binance says fake job adverts tricked one engineer into downloading malicious code before last month's record hack.

The takeaway: a real employer never needs your money or your laptop to say hello.

Send this to someone who's job hunting.

“Nigerian founders need to stop building fintechs. There are too many fintechs already”. 
This is a conversation that comes up almost every eke market day on Nigerian Tech Twitter. Oh “Opay and Moniepoint have already won” “You people are just wasting your time building fintechs”. “The market is already saturated”........And the list goes on and on. 

It is true that everyone is building fintechs. It is true that Opay and Moniepoint have seemingly won the market. What isn't true is that founders building fintechs are wasting their time because Nigerians won't use new fintechs. 

Over the past weeks, we’ve been taking a payment app into the market, businesses and residential communities. We have spoken to merchants, business owners, young people, older people and everyday users. (Please see profile to see Live Field Research Dashboard). 

One thing has become clear in our deployment, Nigerians don’t necessarily reject new fintech because they already have Opay, Moniepoint, or another banking app. Their willingness to try something new often depends on what that product can do for them, what it doesn’t currently offer, and what they stand to gain from using it.

Following a brutal month-long washout across the technology and AI sectors, memory and storage giant SanDisk Corporation (NASDAQ: SNDK) has finally reached a compelling technical bottom, sparking heavy institutional accumulation. On November 9, 2026, SNDK surged 6.16% to close at $886.51. Coming off a massive 50%+ peak-to-trough haircut, a perfect storm of technical oversold conditions, robust fundamentals, and an upcoming high-impact corporate catalyst has fully primed the stock for a violent short-term squeeze.

1. Extreme Oversold Conditions and Aggressive Short Covering

Since peaking in late September, SNDK has been hit by a wave of sector-wide de-risking and post-election policy anxieties, cascade-falling from its all-time highs to a recent low of $803.97.
This near-vertical capitulation has pushed key technical indicators into extreme oversold territory. However, the price action on November 6 and November 9 revealed massive high-volume engulfing green candles, indicating that panic selling has thoroughly exhausted itself. Multi-million dollar institutional blocks have begun aggressively bidding at the $800 psychological support floor, while high implied volatility (IV) reflects heavy call-option loading. A near-term technical mean reversion is now highly asymmetric to the upside.

2. Bulletproof AI Fundamentals: Data Center Demand Remains Unshaken

The preceding sell-off was largely driven by macro anxiety over the sustainability of AI infrastructure capital expenditures. Yet, SanDisk’s actual financial reality paints a completely different, highly bullish picture:
• Massive Top and Bottom Line Beat: In its latest earnings report, SanDisk posted a jaw-dropping 378% year-over-year revenue explosion to $11.03 billion (beating consensus estimates of $107.2 billion), with a Non-GAAP EPS of $49.51.
• Unprecedented Profitability: Driven by its proprietary vertical integration model, the company’s Non-GAAP gross margin expanded to an industry-leading 85.1%.
• Strong Forward Guidance: Management projected next-quarter revenues to scale further to between $12.2 billion and $12.6 billion.
With the stock's trailing P/E multiple compressed to a bargain-basement level of roughly 6.5x, Wall Street heavyweights like JPMorgan have reiterated that the market has excessively penalized this structural AI winner.

3. The Ultimate Near-Term Catalyst: Upcoming 1-for-8 Stock Split

Beyond fundamental valuation, SanDisk possesses a massive sentiment-driven catalyst right around the corner. The company has officially cleared a 1-for-8 forward stock split, set to take effect after the market close on November 19, 2026 (trading split-adjusted on November 20).
While stock splits do not alter intrinsic corporate value, historical data from mega-cap tech peers shows they act as major liquidity magnets. Lowering the nominal share price from nearly $900 down to the $110 range will drastically lower the barrier to entry for retail capital and options market makers, creating a potent immediate-term tailwind to fuel the rebound.

SanDisk's recent drop was a textbook case of over-correction in a nervous market. Backed by explosive earnings growth, an undisputed moat in AI data centers, and a highly anticipated stock split, the downside for SNDK appears firmly capped at $800. For traders and tactical investors looking to capitalize on tech sector rotation, current levels offer a rare, high-conviction buying opportunity.

text:
𝗦𝘁𝗲𝘃𝗲 𝗡𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗼𝗻'𝘀 𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗸 𝗼𝗻 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗠𝗢𝗩𝗜𝗘

The talk Steve Nallon gives on the action movie genre (with DIE HARD as the focal example) covers the appeal of the genre, its history, the psychology of the audience when watching an action movie, the nature of the hero, the setting and arena of the tale, the strategic nature of the plotting, and the genre’s political and social undertones. Steve’s lecture argues that the action movie is a genre largely ignored by academics, generally undervalued by critics, and often even scorned by those who work in the film industry. However, it has proved to be the most commercially successful genre in movie history and, when done well, is one of the few genres that will guarantee a packed audience of the paying public. Indeed, for many, it is the only genre that will get them to leave their house and go to a cinema (Steven Spielberg is said to have told Tom Cruise that TOP GUN: MAVERICK “saved Hollywood’s ass” and might have also “saved the entire theatrical industry”). Yet the talk argues that, despite the commercial rewards of the action movie, it is still one of the most difficult genres to write and make work.
The lecture begins by asking ‘What is meant by “action”?’ and traces the idea and its dramatic usage right back to Aristotle and his POETICS. The talk then takes various concepts of what we call action, such as purpose, desire, plan, project and plot, and argues that clarity in the action line, and how it is manifested in a physical and strategic manner, is essential to the success of any action movie. And in tandem with this goes the ability to create a situation in which that action drive can be developed in an imaginative and original way.
The lecture then moves on to ask, ‘What is the special appeal of the action genre?’ Here the talk looks at the verisimilitude of cinema compared with other media such as the novel, stage, and radio, and suggests that creating what at least looks like actuality is a key aspect of the genre. The talk also examines the pleasure of plot, proposing that the action genre, as with the caper movie and the whodunnit, puts much emphasis on the strategy of the plot, especially its twists and reveals. It is in this sense that the creativity of the action movie is so much underrated and undervalued by academics, critics, and even industry professionals. The talk considers, too, the importance of the ‘rooting interest’ and the empathetic sense of danger that is experienced when watching an action movie. The physiology and psychology of the audience is, the talk argues, one of the key elements that is often overlooked when considering the genre. Far more active involvement is going on than is traditionally proposed. 
The lecture next looks at the action genre in the context of ‘shame culture’, an anthropological term defining a way of thinking that puts great emphasis on the importance of doing the right thing based on the shame you would feel if you didn’t. The lecture points out that the lone hero in the Western – the ultimate ‘shame culture’ movie genre, where “A man’s gotta do what a man’s gotta do” – has certain similarities with the action movie and, to some degree, the action movie developed from that genre.  
With all these thoughts in mind, the talk takes a detailed look at what many regard as the greatest of all action movies, namely, the first DIE HARD picture. It examines the movie’s strategic action, its audience appeal, and the protagonist’s connection to the traditional anti-hero found in the Western. Nor does the talk forget the movie’s humour. There’s a look, as well, at the social context of the 1980s with regard to DIE HARD. The talk considers, for example, the perceived threat to masculinity inherent in several notable 1980s movies, such as FATAL ATTRACTION, FIRST BLOOD, and THE WAR OF THE ROSES. John McClane in DIE HARD is estranged from his wife, who has taken a lucrative job where she is second in command of a multinational company, and so he is facing a life of loss without a defined domestic role. The movie also taps into the sense of loss of standing in America at the time, and indeed in Hollywood itself, where Japanese tech companies such as Sony were aggressively buying up and taking over film studios. The tower building in DIE HARD, it should be noted, may be in LA, but it is owned by Japan. Not only that, but the gang with all the know-how are German, and they easily manage to outwit the FBI agents. Furthermore, the Everyman characters, John McClane and Sergeant Al Powell (who in America doesn’t know a guy named Al?) are ignored and sidelined by the powers that be. It is in this context that the talk suggest that below the surface of the explosive action and the strategies and counter-strategies lie complex social, psychological and political subtexts – and it is these undercurrents that make DIE HARD such a quintessentially 1980s movie from a twenty-first century perspective. 
The next section of the lecture examines in detail some of the creative issues in developing and writing an action movie screenplay. One problem is giving the hero depth of character. That said, there is perhaps a larger range of heroes in the action movie genre than you might at first imagine. These include the anti-hero (MAD MAX, ESCAPE FROM NEW YORK); the rogue hero (LETHAL WEAPON, DIRTY HARRY, TOP GUN, and the recent sequel TOP GUN: MAVERICK); the comedy/trickster hero (BEVERLY HILLS COP, PIRATES OF THE CARIBBEAN); and the travelling angel hero (THE EQUALIZER, FISTFUL OF DOLLARS). The lecture suggests that John McClane is a rich combination of all these different types of hero, which in part explains his iconic appeal. Another issue is the justification for what the hero does, which in screenwriting is known as the ‘warrant for action’, meaning, in the context of an action movie, the use of violence as a justifiable force in the event of some sort of threat or attack. With regard to this point, the lecture looks at the issue of buildings being blown up in action movies following the events of 9/11. The talk points out that the genre, perhaps wanting to avoid the politics and ramifications of actual real-life terrorism, turned to sci-fi and alien invasions as the primary warrant for action. That said, contemporary social and political undertones can still be found in the action movie, notably in WAR OF THE WORLDS and INDEPENDENCE DAY. 
The lecture next examines the ‘arena of conflict’ in an action movie, meaning both the setting and the nature of the forces of antagonism. Some action movies involve a moving arena (RAIDERS OF THE LOST ARK, STAR WARS); in others, the arena is completely enclosed and sometimes contracting (AIRPORT, TOWERING INFERNO, POSEIDON ADVENTURE). Similarly, the forces of antagonism can be singular (THE TERMINATOR, PREDATOR) or multiple (THE MATRIX). DIE HARD, the lecture points out, has a changing arena, but also one that is enclosed. And again, the psychology of the audience is addressed here, with special consideration of the fear of enclosed spaces and natural resistance to the unnatural experience of flying or diving. Then, there are the multiple forces of antagonism, where conflict comes not just from the gang and the building’s environment, but also from those who should be on your side – namely the FBI. 
The lecture then moves on to consider one of the most misunderstood aspects of the action genre, specifically the conflict of the forces of opposition. The talk argues that, in the action genre, the ‘protagonist’ is not necessarily the ‘hero’. Strictly speaking, the protagonist is the one with the initial action-plan, whereas it is the antagonist who comes up with the counter-action. In DIE HARD, the villain is, therefore, the ‘protagonist’ and the hero, John McClane, is the ‘antagonist’. And it is both the imaginative strategy of the protagonist-villain (it is a quite brilliant plan with a great twist) and the inventive countering of that plan by the antagonist-hero (“Now I have a machine gun. Ho-ho-ho!”) that give so much dramatic pleasure in the movie. Related to all this physical and psychological plotting is the fact that it is based on a comprehensive understanding of the principles and stratagems of warfare. One particular aspect worth mentioning here is the stratagem of jungle warfare. The film-makers knowingly created DIE HARD as a ‘jungle picture’, in the sense that the world of the urban building, unfinished and still under construction, often takes on the appearance of an obstacle-laden jungle environment.
Next, the lecture traces the history of the action genre back to the early Westerns, but argues that the first recognisable ‘action movie’ was GUNGA DIN in 1939. The talk illustrates how, in the action genre, certain compulsory scenes have become a necessary feature. These include an initial non-violent confrontation between villain and hero, and later the perilous situation when the hero is at the mercy of the villain – with the reversal that the hero, through ingenuity, ultimately triumphs. Such scenes can be found in a whole array of action movies, including CON AIR, RAIDERS OF THE LOST ARK, HEAT, TRUE LIES, JEWEL IN THE NILE, and, most notably, the 007 Bond franchise. There are also action movies such as BLADE RUNNER where the boundaries of hero and villain are somewhat blurred, resulting in scenes that are subverted and ambiguous. 
The final section of the talk anticipates the changes and developments that might be possible in the action movie genre in the future. More female ‘heroes’ of the action movie could emerge, encouraged by movies such as ALIEN and LARA CROFT. Satire and comedy may also become a means of developing the genre, as might animation. Despite the action movie being seen as violent, it is interesting to note the number of heroes in the genre who transcend or eschew violence, as seen in films like BLADE RUNNER, HACKSAW RIDGE, THE FUGITIVE, MULAN, PRINCESS BRIDE, and even STAR WARS. The irony of the action genre is that its future may lie in a value system where non-violence becomes the primary means of overcoming an initially violent action – or not, as the case may be.
Steve Nallon offers a variety of talks on movie history, film genres, and cinematic techniques. Presentations are available for literary festivals, cultural societies, schools, colleges, libraries, museums, cruises, and film clubs.

Three points on this, the conciliatory first:

1) yes, there undoubtedly is a campaign that is primarily driven by interest in/animus towards Israel, and input into the Myanmar case has become part of that; the Irish intervention is I guess a valid example of that

2) there is however, besides that, undoubtedly indeed a “theoretical argument” that PRECEDES the Israel case and has nothing whatsoever to do with Israel at all. To understand this, eg read the UK/GER etc intervention from Nov 2023 (again, all very pro-Israel at that time and filed well before the SA case even existed): https://t.co/wNYqr9UCOL

3) if you want to make the case for 1), it’s actually not a good idea to do so while completely ignoring, or being ignorant of, 2); or making clearly absurd claims like that the order of the Myanmar and Israel rulings is driven by that (it’s not. Myanmars case is four years older. It was always going to be decided first). 

And as for “not a clean legal case”, well, does such a thing exist? Ask whether Likud voters think the Israeli Supreme Court is delivering “clean legal cases”. As for the judges, one of them is Julia Sebutinde, who is on record(!) saying “The Lord is counting on me to stand on the side of Israel”. There’s no other judge who has offered an even remotely comparable biased statement in the other direction. And if you read some of the earlier declarations and orders from the court it’s clear they and the court is seriously grappling and engaging with the issues, not just rubber stamping pre formed opinions, eg Judge Nolte in his declaration on the second provisional measures order: https://t.co/kCpUS0EVuA

text:
I moderated the panel on AI as a Colleague: Redefining Roles, Power and Productivity at the Scottish Ethnic Minority Talent Summit and Festival.

We discussed and debated ideas around AI and the skills gap. One of the things the panel centred on was the need to upskill people to enjoy and take advantage of the dividends of AI. At the centre of AI is the ability to go in-depth into your field.

There is a need to build a core understanding and depth in your field to harness the potential AI has to offer. There was a reflection on whether AI would replace entry-level roles, and at the centre of that debate was the fact that young people are still needed in the workforce. There are important skills to learn as an entry-level staff member that are deeply human and that aid learning and drive economic growth. We cannot replace those skills, or totally replace them with AI. So, we need to maintain our entry-level pipeline while AI can serve as a co-intelligence to drive work productivity. We can’t just AI our way to economic growth and development at the expense of our young people, who need the opportunity and space to develop core skills in the workplace and grow as well.

There was also the need to go back to core skills like critical thinking and make sure they are at the centre of learning because someone who can think critically would also use AI critically. In the same way, someone who understands the nitty-gritty of a business may be able to optimise their business using AI because of the foundational knowledge they already possess. So, we shouldn't lose the opportunity to build depth at the expense of AI.

There were a few debates on company culture around the use of AI and how leadership and culture can determine how open colleagues are about using AI.

We couldn’t cover all the ground, but it was great to share the space with Andreas and Anne, who shared incredible thoughts and contributed to the discourse. We definitely missed Dr Pallvi on the panel, and hopefully, we can reconnect again sometime soon.

Thanks to Fash Fashoro, Azeem Adeyemi and Odunayo Ogunsanwo, and the volunteers of Datakirk, for organising an incredible summit and festival. It was great to connect with students and professionals who were passionate about tech and AI, share my journey into that space with them, and have some of our scholars at the Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program at the University of Edinburgh present there.

I am usually the speaker at events, but it was great to be on the other side, moderating.

WHAT I'M WATCHING TODAY — TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 10, 2026
U.S. inflation takes centre stage today, but my biggest earnings focus is CoreWeave $CRWV.
Both will help answer a question I've been following closely: can the AI infrastructure buildout deliver attractive returns when financing costs remain elevated?
U.S. MACRO — ET
🔹 4:00 AM — Fed Waller Speech
🔹 6:00 AM — NFIB Business Optimism: 97.7 Est. vs 97.9 Previous
🔹 8:30 AM — October CPI Report
🔹 Core CPI MoM: +0.2% Est. vs +0.3% Previous
🔹 Headline CPI MoM: +0.3% Est. vs +0.6% Previous

THE INFLATION QUESTION
Monthly core inflation is expected to slow to 0.2%, while headline inflation is projected to ease from 0.6% to 0.3%.
One important complication: the BLS is not expected to publish annual headline and core CPI rates for October because comparable October 2025 price data are unavailable.
That makes the monthly readings and underlying components particularly important.
I'll be watching shelter, services, goods inflation and Treasury yields to see how markets adjust their expectations for Fed policy.
For capital-intensive businesses, the transmission matters:
Inflation → Fed expectations → Treasury yields → Financing costs.
Lower financing costs help, but they cannot make an uneconomic project profitable.
UK — GMT
🔹 1:30 PM — BoE Lombardelli Speech
🔹 7:30 PM — BoE Pill Speech
EARNINGS — BEFORE THE BELL
🔹 $QBTS — D-Wave Quantum
🔹 $SE — Sea Limited
🔹 $ONON — On Holding
🔹 $WIX — https://t.co/sQUyXkD4p4

🔹 $TDG — TransDigm
🔹 $PDYN — Palladyne AI
🔹 $HMC — Honda
🔹 $CAN — Canaan
EARNINGS — AFTER THE CLOSE
🔹 $CRWV — CoreWeave
🔹 $RGTI — Rigetti Computing
🔹 $AMPX — Amprius Technologies
🔹 $FLY — Firefly Aerospace
🔹 $PBR / $PBRA — Petrobras
🔹 $LPTH — LightPath Technologies
🔹 $LWLG — Lightwave Logic
MY MAIN FOCUS
1. AI INFRASTRUCTURE — $CRWV, $BTDR, $WYFI
CoreWeave is my biggest earnings focus today.
I'll be watching contracted demand, capacity deployment, customer concentration, debt financing, margins and free cash flow.
The question isn't whether AI demand exists. It's whether that demand can generate attractive returns after financing costs and capital expenditure.
I want to see how quickly contracted capacity becomes utilised capacity, recognised revenue and ultimately cash generation.
2. QUANTUM COMPUTING — $QBTS, $RGTI
D-Wave and Rigetti offer another test of the gap between technological progress and commercial economics.
I'll be comparing revenue growth, customer adoption, cash burn and funding requirements.
The technology may be advancing, but investors still need evidence of a sustainable commercial model.
3. ADVANCED TECHNOLOGY — $AMPX, $PDYN, $KULR
I'll be looking for evidence that product development and partnerships are translating into orders, recognised revenue and improving margins.
The distinction between announcements and actual commercial execution matters.
4. CONSUMER & DIGITAL PLATFORMS — $SE, $ONON, $WIX, $ETOR
The focus is revenue growth, operating leverage, customer activity and cash generation.
I'll be watching whether these businesses can sustain growth without sacrificing profitability.
5. ENERGY & INDUSTRIALS — $VG, $PBR, $TDG
I'll be watching energy demand, pricing, capital allocation, project economics and aerospace margins.
For energy businesses, investment discipline matters just as much as demand growth.
MY TAKE
I'm still bullish on the long-term opportunities across AI infrastructure, semiconductors and emerging technologies.
But strong demand doesn't automatically translate into strong shareholder returns.
CoreWeave sits at the centre of that debate. Its earnings should offer another opportunity to assess whether AI infrastructure spending is moving towards sustainable cash generation.
Quantum computing faces an earlier-stage challenge: turning technological progress into meaningful commercial revenue without excessive dilution.
And today's inflation report matters because the cost of capital remains an important part of that investment equation.
WHAT MATTERS NEXT
Inflation → Fed policy → Treasury yields → Cost of capital
AI demand → Capacity deployment → Utilisation → Revenue
Revenue → Margins → Free cash flow → Returns on invested capital
That's what I'll be watching as the data and earnings come through today.

text:
**5000$ Earnings with Google! 

 Earnings are realistic but usually require consistent effort, traffic, or skills—there are no get-rich-quick shortcuts. Avoid scams promising easy cash just for searching or clicking.

### 1. Google AdSense (Website/Blog Monetization)
Display ads on your site and earn when people view or click them.

- **How it works**: Apply, get approved, add ad code. Google matches relevant ads.
- **Requirements**: Age 18+, own/control a site with high-quality original content that attracts an audience, comply with policies. No official minimum traffic or post count.(<https://t.co/Wl6pRoqVx2>)
- **Earnings**: Highly variable—often $50–$500+/month for growing sites; $1,000+ possible with strong traffic and high-CPC niches (finance, tech, etc.). Payout threshold is typically $100 USD (or local equivalent); payments issued around the 21st–26th of the following month.(<https://t.co/zt7r2OejVR>)
- **Tips**: Focus on SEO for organic Google traffic. Combine with affiliate marketing.

### 2. YouTube Partner Program
Monetize videos with ads, memberships, Super Chat, and more.

- **How it works**: Grow a channel, apply once you meet thresholds, link AdSense.
- **Requirements (2026)**: 1,000 subscribers + 4,000 valid watch hours (last 12 months) or 10 million Shorts views (last 90 days). Fan-funding features unlock earlier (around 500 subs + lower thresholds). Note: thresholds double for new applicants starting February 1, 2027.(<https://t.co/TozDnVBJxf>)
- **Earnings**: Creators keep ~55% of net long-form ad revenue (45% for Shorts). Typical RPM (revenue per 1,000 views) is roughly $2–$12 depending on niche, audience location, and engagement. Larger channels can earn thousands monthly many start smaller.(<https://t.co/xPuc5DcaTK>)
- **Tips**: Consistent uploads + SEO (titles, thumbnails, descriptions) help. Sponsorships and affiliates work even before full monetization.

### 3. Freelance Google Skills
Offer services that businesses pay for:

- **Google Ads management** (PPC campaigns)
- **SEO specialist** (ranking sites in Google search)
- **Google Analytics / data analysis**
- **Google Business Profile** (local SEO / Google Maps optimization)
- **Google Workspace admin** or setup

Rates commonly range from $20–$150+/hour depending on experience and location. Start with free Google Skillshop certifications and small clients.(<https://t.co/gERERsuSrA>)

### 4. Search Engine / Quality Evaluator (Contract Work)
Rate search results, ads, or AI outputs for Google contractors (e.g., TELUS International, Appen/CrowdGen, Welo Data).

- Typical pay: roughly $10–$20+/hour depending on country, role, and project (higher in US/Europe; lower elsewhere). Work is part-time and task-based.
- Apply through official contractor sites—watch for fakes.(<https://t.co/KdO7al5Vbn>)

### 5. Other Options
- **Google Play / AdMob**: Build and monetize Android apps (ads, in-app purchases, paid apps).
- **Google Opinion Rewards**: Short surveys for small Google Play/PayPal credits (side income only).
- **E-commerce / affiliate**: Use Google Shopping, organic search, or Google Ads to drive sales of products or affiliate offers.
- **Digital products / courses**: Sell via your site or Google tools and drive traffic with SEO.

### Realistic Expectations
Building traffic (AdSense/YouTube) often takes months of consistent work. Skill-based freelancing or evaluator work can start faster. Track results, reinvest early earnings, and diversify. Official resources: https://t.co/lsVmRr7J3t, https://t.co/XJavNYLkZ5, and Google Skillshop.

Start with one method that matches your skills (writing, video, technical, or local services). Consistency matters more than any single trick.

In connection with information that has appeared in the media in recent days regarding a possible delivery of L-39 Skyfox aircraft to Serbia, we would like to clarify certain facts and provide broader context regarding the ongoing negotiations.
First and foremost, we would like to express our appreciation for the support of the Czech Government and Prime Minister Andrej Babiš personally in promoting Czech companies abroad and helping open new business opportunities. For AERO, which exports a significant share of its production to international markets, such support is extremely important and highly valued.
We can confirm that, through the Prime Minister, we presented the Serbian side with a specific proposal for the supply of L-39 Skyfox aircraft during his official visit to Serbia. Our offer was received very positively, and discussions have since advanced significantly. Both parties are currently working to resolve the remaining technical, commercial, and financial matters.
This is a strategically important project for both sides, encompassing not only the aircraft themselves but also a wide range of related technical, operational, and contractual issues. For projects of this scale, it is entirely standard for the process, from the submission of an offer through the negotiation of individual terms to the signing of a contract, to take several months.
We would therefore like to emphasize that the negotiations are proceeding in a standard manner and within the usual timeframe. Specific technical, commercial, and contractual matters are being addressed directly between AERO and the relevant Serbian partners. It is therefore natural that not every intermediate step or detail is continuously shared at the political level.
We believe that the distinction between the advanced stage of commercial negotiations and the actual signing of a contract may have led to certain inaccurate or incomplete interpretations that subsequently appeared in the public domain.
We are confident in the quality of our offer and in the benefits that the L-39 Skyfox can bring to the Serbian Air Force. We view the progress of the negotiations very positively and remain optimistic that they will be successfully concluded in the near future.
Given the ongoing commercial discussions, we do not consider it appropriate to disclose further details at this stage. We will inform the public of the outcome as soon as circumstances permit.

text:
The Alt Centrist Approach To Generational Relations

For many centuries, generational relations have been simple. Older people worked to take care of the young, and then when the young grew up they took care of the old. Everyone had a turn at helping and at being helped. This all ended with the Boomers. The Boomers took their turn at being helped, and then ripped up the social contract to run society exclusively for their short-term benefit.

The old systems worked on the basis that the elderly would teach the young wisdom. The problem today is that today’s elderly have little wisdom to teach. The elderly of previous generations had survived wars and great depressions, and taught the following generations not to trust authorities and to think for themselves. The Boomers, by contrast, teach that if it wasn’t true, they wouldn’t be allowed to say it on television.

The approach of the Establishment up until now has been to offer old people the fattest and most luxurious pensions possible. Pensioners in France receive more money on average than the average working-age adult. So when it comes to distributive justice, Boomers take the lion’s share, and the people that actually build and maintain society live off the scraps. This has led to stagnation, a violation of the First Rejection.

The Boomer-first approach also violates the First Acceptance by leading to revolution. Long-term societal order is predicated on fairness; without fairness, the disadvantaged become resentful and begin to support an overthrow of the existing social order. So far, television, smartphones, pharmaceuticals and cheap protein have combined to limit revolutionary fervour. But the housing situation has become so bad in the West that true hatred of Boomers is starting to appear in the hearts of Gen Z and some Millennials.

The alt centrist does not believe in impoverishing old people. But they must not have luxuries at the expense of the young. This is why the alternative centrist approach to generational relations involves cutting pensions to the level of unemployed young people. No state pension should be higher than the lowest unemployment benefit.

The idea that old people have been promised luxury pensions, and therefore they have the right to force young people to pay for them, is utterly rejected. The idea that the pension age is a ‘finish line’ at which people can stop contributing and get waited on by the young is also rejected. The universal basic income (see The Alt Centrist Approach To Welfare) puts an upper limit on the extent of the welfare burden that old people can impose on the young.

The healthcare burden would be limited as well. The alternative centrist approach is to rapidly euthanise anyone old and sick enough to become a significant expense. In the past, dementia patients were kept alive in the hope some miracle cure would be found. This was not a major problem because other conditions killed the vast majority of people before they could develop dementia. It is believed that global costs of dementia will hit USD2.8 trillion by 2030. In New Zealand alone the costs are billions of dollars annually.

All this misery and expense would be prevented by an alternative centrist government under the Fourth Rejection. It is cruel to keep dementia patients alive in the vain hope of a miracle cure, and thus they would be euthanised.

Already those aged 65 or over consume half of all healthcare expenditure in New Zealand. The cited report claims “The average 85 year old uses 16 times more healthcare than the average 40 year old.” Much of this expense goes to cancer treatment, which can keep old people alive for decades beyond their natural life span. The alternative centrist opposes spending billions on lost causes. Thus we support euthanasia for old people riddled with cancer.

The combined cost of pensions and healthcare represent a titanic burden on younger generations. The alternative centrist would remove it and let younger people breathe freely.

Generational relations have chiefly been destroyed by the unwillingness of Boomers to have children, and to contribute to raising them. If there are no younger generations, there are no generational relations. Birth rates collapsed when the Boomers hit adulthood and decided to drink booze instead of raise families. Ultimately, today’s problem with generational relations all come down to monumental selfishness on the part of Boomers. Boomers are a Cluster B personality disorder on the scale of an entire generation.

This selfishness is all downstream of the philosophical approach of Boomers, which is nihilistic, atheist and materialistic, suggesting that life has no meaning other than to consume. Therefore, much of the solution to poor generational relations is spiritual (see The Alt Centrist Approach To Spirituality).

A properly spiritual approach will teach people that they are all part of the natural cycle of birth, maturity and death. It would also teach people about karma, and therefore that selfishness towards the young will be reciprocated in a future life.

In a state of Nature, people incarnate into their bodies and think they are their bodies, doomed to die. Over time, some wake up and realise they are fragments of God consciousness, eternal and invincible, and that’s there’s nothing to worry about. Usually these people are old, because it takes time to wake up, which is why most of the various teachers and gurus that are well known to history are old. So in an alternative centrist state, the post-Boomer elderly would be strongly encouraged and incentivised to teach spiritual lessons to younger generations. The middle-aged and the young can deal with the material world, with business, manufacturing, retail, law enforcement etc. The elderly would be taught that they were earning a more auspicious rebirth this way.

In summary, generational relations today are coloured by the extreme selfishness and narcissism of the Boomers. The alternative centrist belief is that the following generations will be comparatively normal, and therefore generational relations will be close to normal. Once normalised, the old can be encouraged to raise the young rather than exploit them.

text:
They cut off a buffalo's head for rain, then let its body roll away! 🐃

✍🏻 *Post 14 | 10 November '26*
💭 *Topic — Lokdharma*
──────────

Chui village in the Ranapur area of Jhabua district, Madhya Pradesh. Here, around Diwali, people gather on the hill of Baba Dev to learn how the rains and farming will go in the coming year.

But the method is not checking weather statistics. After the puja, a buffalo is sacrificed and its headless body is rolled down the hill.

📍 *Locally, this practice is called "Paada Parampara".* Here, "paada" refers to a male buffalo.

It is believed that how far the body rolls, how fast it goes, and whether it stops midway can be used to predict the rains and crops. Local elders interpret these signs and tell people what the next year will be like.

📹 *The C B Live report of 22 October 2025* describes thousands of people gathering, the puja, and the body being rolled down after the sacrifice. At that event, good rains and a good harvest were predicted for 2026.

🪘 The reports also mention drums and the collective gathering. So this is not just one person's belief; it is a community practice carried forward for generations. According to the Agniban report, women are not allowed to go up the hill; they watch the event from below.

This is described as a tradition handed down from ancestors. However, the available reports do not give a verified year of its origin or any historical reason for it.

🌧️ Rain is truly important for farming. But the reports do not provide any scientific evidence linking a dead animal's body rolling down with the next year's rainfall. In trying to know the weather through belief, an animal's life is certainly lost.

🪞 *Our concern is the future, so why should the buffalo pay the price?*

Superstition promises that a ritual will give an answer to uncertainty. It spares you the difficulty of testing your belief, and the loss falls on another living being.

If sacrifice means giving up your attachment, then the question is about the grip of your own fear, greed and ego. But here, your own grip remains intact, and another's body is offered up instead.

❓ *When violence appears in a tradition, what am I trying to protect?*

A. Our elders did it, so it must be right.

B. If I give it up, something bad might happen.

C. If I raise a question, my own people will get angry.

D. I worry more about my belief breaking than about the animal's suffering.

✍🏻 *Which belief am I afraid to examine, and why?*

text:
EPISODE 9 – THE KISS

After returning from the conference, Victoria and Daniel have a serious argument.

Daniel accuses her of being emotionally unavailable.

Victoria tells him their marriage has been broken for years.

Meanwhile, Mara receives an offer from another company.

She decides to resign.

She enters Victoria’s office and places her resignation letter on the desk.

Victoria reads it.

“You’re leaving?”

“Yes.”

“Because of me?”

Mara takes a deep breath.

“Because I cannot keep working somewhere I feel unwanted and humiliated.”

Victoria stands up.

“I never wanted you to feel that way.”

Mara laughs bitterly.

“Then you should have treated me differently.”

Victoria walks around the desk.

For the first time, she stops pretending.

“I was afraid.”

“Afraid of what?”

Victoria looks at her.

“Of wanting you.”

Mara freezes.

Victoria continues.

“I thought if I made things difficult enough, you would stop looking at me that way. I thought I could make these feelings disappear.”

Mara whispers:

“And did they?”

Victoria shakes her head.

“No.”

There is a long silence.

Mara moves closer.

Victoria looks at her lips.

And then they kiss.

It is brief, emotional and completely unexpected.

When they separate, Victoria looks terrified.

Mara whispers:

“Victoria…”

Victoria steps back.

“Please go home.”

text:
A CRUEL KIND OF LOVE 

SEASON 1 CONTINUATION 

EPISODE 6 – THE WOMAN AT HOME

The audience gets a deeper look into Victoria’s marriage.

Daniel has been having an affair with a woman named Rebecca for almost a year.

Victoria knows about it but has chosen to ignore it because of their business partnership and public image.

Meanwhile, Mara begins distancing herself from Victoria.

She stops volunteering for extra assignments and starts applying for other jobs.

Victoria notices immediately.

She asks Mara why she has become distant.

Mara replies that she is simply trying to maintain professional boundaries.

Victoria doesn’t like the answer.

During a heated conversation, she says:

“Is this because of what happened between us?”

Mara responds:

“Nothing happened between us, Victoria. That’s the problem.”

Victoria is left speechless.

            THE NEW MAN

Adrian Cole joins the company as creative director.

He immediately develops an interest in Mara.

Unlike Victoria, Adrian is friendly and approachable.

He invites Mara to lunch, makes her laugh and appreciates her work.

Victoria notices their growing friendship.

During a meeting, she interrupts Adrian several times when he praises Mara.

Later, she asks Mara to remain behind.

“Are you involved with Adrian?”

Mara is confused.

“Excuse me?”

“I asked whether you’re seeing him.”

“That’s none of your business.”

Victoria looks offended.

Mara realizes what she has said and continues.

“You don’t get to control my personal life because you don’t know how to handle yours.”

She leaves.

Victoria is furious, but underneath her anger is something she cannot admit.

Jealousy.
